The hum had been a constant, a fact, like the tide. Its absence was a new fact, and facts you haven't learned to live with feel like holes in the floor. The news came in through the pub, where Calloway went most afternoons to sit with his tea and watch the television that still worked, mostly. The speech was being argued about everywhere now. The survey woman, whose name I'd never learned but who went by "Dr. something" on the broadcasts, had recorded the audio, and the audio was being parsed by teams of people in rooms I couldn't imagine. One channel had a man with a suit and a serious face saying the structures were "likely broadcasting a territorial claim." Another had a woman with a soft voice saying it was "consistent with ancient human prayers, specifically from the Mesopotamian region, though the translation is speculative." Calloway turned the volume up and pointed at the screen. "Territorial claim. He's saying they're marking us like we're their property." "Or they're saying the water belongs to them," I said. "That's not the same thing." "It might be, if they think the water and the land are the same." He looked at me. He was the kind of man who appreciated simple explanations the way I appreciated complicated ones, we were opposites in this regard, and he'd known it for thirty years without ever saying so. He poured more tea and said, "So what does that mean for us?" "I don't know." "My traps are full of nothing. My nets are hanging in the barn. I've got a tractor that needs a new belt and no reason to run it." He drank his tea. "The mainland says to stay home. The mainland says don't approach the structures. The mainland says the situation is being monitored." "Is it being monitored from here?" "Nobody's coming here to monitor anything. I checked the harbor. No boats, no planes, no one with a sign on the side of anything. Just us." The cousin call came that week. My cousin Davie, who lived in Inverness and who had been sending me postcards since before I could read them properly, had a message waiting when the phone rang, because he had finally gotten through to me after calling every day for a week. "Get off the island," he said, without preamble. "That's not a suggestion. The council is organizing transport. I've got a van, I can pick you up, you can stay with me until, " "Until what?" "Until this is sorted." "Sorted how?" "I don't know. Until the structures leave. Until the fish come back. Until somebody with a better boat than a skiff figures out what those things are and tells us whether we're alive or not." He paused. "Ren, the structures are still there. A month in and they're still there. That's not an attack. That's an occupation." "The fish are still dying." "Slowly. Not like at first. The flatfish are gone, yes, but I'm hearing that the bigger species are holding on. The cod, the mackerel, they're, " "They're gone too. I caught one live cod last week. That was the last one." He went quiet. The phone crackled with the hum of his kitchen, the sound of a kettle, the distant noise of a town that still had traffic and weather and normal problems. "Come to Inverness," he said again. "Petra can stay too. Mara's already on the mainland. You're the only one holding on." "I've got a boat to maintain." "Maintain it in Inverness." "The sea needs watching." "By you? From a skiff? Ren, you can't see anything from out there now. The water's, " He stopped. Swallowed. "The water's wrong. You said it yourself. I stood in my kitchen with Mara in the shed behind me, reorganizing Callum's boxes into a more efficient configuration, and I listened to Davie breathe, and I thought about the trap line, which was empty, and the mackerel, which were gone, and the flatfish, which had died in July, and the structures, which were silent now and patient and permanent. "I'll think about it," I said. "Think fast." He hung up. I put the phone down and went to the window. The structures were there. Three of them, flat and wide, sitting in the water two miles off the island, unchanged in a month. They didn't block the light anymore, not quite, but they sat in the same spot, and the water around them was that dense, purposeful water, the water with more intention than water should have. Petra came by that evening. She had a bottle of whisky and a bag of bread, which she set on my counter with the efficiency of a woman who had decided to share resources rather than discuss feelings. "The radio said something today," she said, pouring two glasses. "They're sending a ship out. Not a survey ship. Something bigger. They're calling it a dialogue vessel." "A dialogue vessel." "Apparently it's loaded with, " She waved a hand. "Technology. Equipment. They're trying to answer it. To speak back." "That's nice." "It's not nice. It's a gamble. You don't answer a stranger who's said one sentence and then gone quiet. You wait. You see if they come back." "Maybe they're waiting too." "Waiting for what?" I thought about the hum. Petra poured the second glass and handed it to me without saying anything. We stood at the window and watched the structures, which were not waiting, which were not speaking, which were simply there, occupying space in the sea with the same indifference that the sea had shown to the mackerel and the herring and the flatfish that came out of season and died in buckets. It was the last of what Petra had, and she'd saved it for something, and this was as good a something as any. "Stay home," she said. "Let the mainland try their dialogue." "I'll stay home," I said. "For now."

The sink was worse than I'd thought. The seal had rotted through, and there was a slow drip into the cabinet that had swollen the wood, which was why I'd been avoiding it. Not the leak itself. Mara stood over me with a flashlight, not helping, just witnessing, and when I tightened the last fitting she said, "That took you a year." "The sea was busy." "You don't fish anymore." "Something was busy." She turned off the flashlight. We stood in the kitchen with the leak stopped and the hall full of boxes and the structures visible through the window, their faint glow making the sea look like a road that went somewhere nobody was going. Mara went to the counter and opened a box, Callum's, she was getting through them one at a time, and she pulled out a photo album. She didn't look at it. She set it on the table where it lay open to a page with a photograph of her as a girl, eight years old, standing in the bait shop with Petra's hand on her shoulder, grinning with her whole face, the way children do before they learn that grinning at full volume is something adults do and children do only in pictures. "I used to ask her questions," Mara said. "About the fish. About the seasons. Why the flatfish came in August. Why the water was warmer in the cove than at the point." "Petra liked that." "She told me things no one else would. She told me the sea was like a library, and the fish were the books, and the seasons were the reading order." She closed the album. "She never told me why I left." "You left for your degree." "I left because I wanted to be somewhere where the questions were answered. Where a university would tell me why the flatfish come in August instead of a woman in rubber boots saying 'the water remembers.'" She looked at me. "You never answered either. You had the same answers, Dad. You just didn't say them out loud." I thought about that. I thought about the mackerel going first, which was the sea's order, which was the sea's library, which was the sea's reading order, and I thought about how I'd known that for thirty-one years and had never once explained it to anyone, because explaining was for people who needed explaining, and I'd assumed the sea spoke for itself. The sea had stopped speaking. Or had stopped being a language I recognized. "There's something in the water," I said. "Not fish. Not yet. But when I went out last week, the net came up with, " I stopped. I hadn't told her this. "There was something in the second trap. Small. Alive. Translucent." "Alive." "Alive. It was the size of a thumb. It had legs, maybe, or arms, I don't know. It moved like a fish but its body was wrong. Like a fish drawn by someone who'd seen fish in a book but never in the water." "Did you keep it?" "I put it back. I put it back in the water and I watched it swim. It went deep, faster than anything I've seen swim." Mara sat down. She was tired, I could see it in her shoulders, the way they held themselves, not slumped but braced, as if carrying something invisible from the hospital ward in Inverness. "Are you scared?" "I'm a fisherman," I said. "I don't have the vocabulary for scared anymore. I have the vocabulary for empty nets." "Empty nets are scared in a way I can't say." She was right. She'd always been right about things she shouldn't have been able to say, about the sea, about Petra, about me. She'd left at nineteen with a head full of questions and had spent twelve years finding answers that didn't include Brough, and now she was back among the boxes, and the answers were worse than the questions. We ate in the kitchen that night. Mara made pasta because she had ingredients in her bag and I had no fish, and she talked about Callum's ward, about the nurse who called him by his middle name, about the garden on the roof where he grew tomatoes he couldn't eat because of the sugar. She talked the way she did when she was comfortable, fast, specific, full of small facts that meant nothing to anyone but her. I listened. I ate the pasta with my fingers, because there was a fork and I could have used it, but the eating was the point, not the utensil. "Stay the week," I said. "The boxes can wait. I'll sort them." She looked at me. Not the teenager's look. Something older, something that had been through a marriage and a father's boat and a month of dead fish and a speech from the structures that said different things to different ears. "Okay," she said. "But you're telling me if anything else comes out of the water." "I'll tell you." "And you're telling me before Petra, or before the news, or before anyone on the mainland decides what I should be told." "I'll tell you first." It was a small promise. It cost me nothing. But she held onto it like it was a trap with bait in it, and I thought maybe that was the point, that the trap was still full, even when the sea was empty.

# Chapter 7: Going Out Anyway I told Mara I was going out. She said, "For what?" and I said, "To see," which was not true, because I'd seen enough, and she said, "The water's dead, Dad," which was also not true, because I'd caught the translucent thing in the second trap, which meant something was still in there, even if it wasn't mackerel. She wanted to come. I said no, not because I was afraid of her, but because the skiff was small and the structures were close and I needed to be a man in a boat, not two people in a boat, because the first version of that story had my grandfather in it, and the second version had my father, and I was not ready for the third to have witnesses. I left before the light was good. The structures were dark from this angle, and the water between them and the island was that dense, purposeful water, the water that moved like it had somewhere to be. My skiff cut through it with a sound that felt wrong, too loud, too present, as if the sea was listening. I spitted over my left shoulder. The structures didn't care. The first trap was empty. The bait was gone, dissolved, as if the water had eaten it rather than the bait having been consumed. I moved to the second. The net came up with water and a single, small, translucent shape that I could see through, that moved with a flickering speed I couldn't follow with my eyes but could feel with my hand as it brushed my wrist. I let it go. I sat in the skiff with the empty net in my lap and looked at the structures, which were close now, close enough that I could see the texture of their surface, which was not metal, not stone, not anything I had a word for. It was smooth and slightly warm, and it was alive in the way that a tide is alive, not conscious, not breathing, but full of intention. I talked. Not to them, exactly. I talked at the water, the way you talk at a river when you're alone on it, not expecting an answer, just needing the speaking to go somewhere other than into the air where it would dissolve. "The mackerel were here in April," I said. "They were here in May. They were here last year, the year before, thirty-one years. I know their numbers. I know their seasons. I know where they nest and where they feed and which currents bring them in." The water moved. The structures hummed, faintly, not the speech-hum, not the rhythm-hum, just the base vibration, the one that had been there since the first day. "The flatfish came in July," I said. "They came out of season. They died out of season. That's not a disease. That's not a spill. Something rearranged the water so that the order was wrong, and the fish couldn't survive the wrong order." I thought about Petra's words. *Your water owes.* I thought about my own. *We are the change in your water.* I thought about Mara hearing "come home" in her dead mother's voice, and how that wasn't a translation of any sentence but a translation of a feeling, a shape the sound made in the particular architecture of her grief. "I'm sorry the mackerel died," I said. "I don't know if that's for me to say. I'm a fisherman. The mackerel were my work. But they were here before you were, and they're gone because of where you are, and that's a fact I can't make myself not feel." The water moved. A small current, warm, passing under the skiff like a hand under a chin. "I don't know what you are," I said. "I don't know what you're doing with the water. I don't know if the fish are coming back or if the water is being rebuilt for something I can't see. But I'm here, and I'm tired, and I've been sitting on a dock for a month eating cold stew with my fingers while the sea went wrong, and I wanted to say something to the thing that's doing it, instead of just watching." The structures didn't respond. There was no speech, no rhythm, no syllables. Just the hum, steady and patient, and the water moving under me with its strange density, and the sky turning from black to grey at the horizon, the first sign that morning was coming and the light would change and the structures would look different, as they always did, as they always would. I pulled the trap line in. Empty. Empty. Empty. I sat in the skiff for a long time, watching the water. It was clear here, in the shadow of the structures, clear enough that I could see the bottom, which was maybe forty feet down, and it was clean, no oil, no foam, just sand and stone and the ordinary detritus of a sea floor. But it was also wrong, in the way a clean floor is wrong in a house that used to be full of furniture. You could see everything, and the seeing was the problem. Something small passed beneath the skiff. Not a fish. A shape, translucent, moving with that flickering urgency, going deep, going fast, going somewhere that the old fish had gone but with a different purpose. I watched it go. I didn't reach for the net. I rowed back to the island in the light that was building, the light that came up behind the structures and turned them into silhouettes, which made them look smaller, which made them look like hills, which made them look like geography, which was the most human thing I could do to them, make them part of the landscape instead of an event. Mara was on the dock when I came in. She had been up since before dark, I could tell by the way she stood, still and braced, the way she stood when Callum's cough was bad and she was deciding whether to worry. "Anything?" she said. "No fish." "I know. What else?" I thought about what else. The translucent thing. The warm current under the skiff. The silence of the structures, which was different from the silence before the speech, which had been waiting-silence, and this was something else, finished-silence, or resting-silence, or the silence of something that had said its piece and was now simply present. "There's something alive in there," I said. "Not fish. Something else. Something small that goes deep and fast." Mara's face did the thing it does when she's processing. Not fear, not wonder. Calculation. She was running the numbers, weighing the information, deciding what this meant for the boxes and the flat and Callum's ward and the rest of her life, which was happening on the mainland while I sat on a dock with a skiff that had nothing to catch. "Are you going out again?" she said. "I'll go out again," I said. "Tomorrow. Or the day after. I don't know what I'm looking for, but I know what I'm not looking for, and that's the dock." She nodded. She picked up a box and carried it toward the shed, and I got out of the skiff and went to the water's edge, and I spitted over my left shoulder at the structures, which were grey now, which were hills now, which were part of the island's horizon in the same way the mainland was part of it, and which would be there tomorrow, and the day after, and the day after that, and which were not going anywhere, and which had killed the mackerel, and which had made the water dense with purpose, and which had spoken one sentence that meant different things to different ears, and which were, for now, silent. I spitted, and the sea took it, and went on being whatever it was.

The passage about making the structures look like hills—"which made them look like hills, which made them look like geography, which was the most human thing I could do to them"—is a nice idea but the chain of "which made them" repetitions becomes slightly mechanical, a stylistic tic that calls attention to itself. # Chapter 8: The Flatfish The flatfish came back on a Thursday in late August, which was correct, which was the season, which should have made no sense given everything that had happened. I was checking the trap line the way I did every other morning, out of habit, out of the need to keep my hands busy with something that had a history. The first trap was empty. The second was empty. The third, which sat in the drop-off where the water was deep and the hum, faint as it was now, still reached, had something in it that moved. Flatfish. Four of them. They were early by a week, which was not nothing, but it was not the wrongness of July, not the out-of-season panic of a fish dying in a bucket on a tractor's wheelbarrow. They were flatfish in August, in the water they belonged to, in the current that brought them in, and they fought the hook the way flatfish do, not hard, just persistently, like they were arguing with the idea of being caught. I sat in the skiff holding four flatfish in a net and felt my eyes burn in a way that had nothing to do with the salt. They were the right color. They were the right weight. Their eyes were cloudy and dull, the way living fish's eyes should be when they're not dead, which was a thing I had forgotten to notice, because for a month I'd been checking fish for clarity, looking for the sharp eyes of the wrongness, and now there was nothing wrong with these eyes. They were just eyes. Just fish eyes. Just the ordinary dull gold of a creature that eats from the bottom and doesn't think about much. I netted them. I put them in the bucket. I rowed in. Petra's shop had its door open. She stood there in her rubber boots with her hands on her hips, the way she did when something was about to happen that she hadn't calculated for, and she saw the bucket and she saw the fish and she did not say anything for a long time. Then she came down the steps and held up one flatfish and turned it over in her hands, looking at the underside, the eyes, the gill movement, the way it flexed with a life that was not the wrong life. "Where'd you catch these?" she said. "Drop-off. Third trap." "Third trap. That's the one nearest the structures." "That's the one with the best light." She set the fish back in the bucket. She looked at me. "They're right." "They're right." "That's not, that's not what I mean. They're right-colored, right-weighted, right-eyed. They're not the translucent things. They're not the pale heavy dead things. They're flatfish." "Flatfish in August. A week early." "A week early." She pressed her hand flat against the bucket, where the fish moved against her palm, pushing back, alive, ordinary, present. "A week early is nothing. A week early is weather. A week early is the sea being the sea." I took them inside the shop. The freezer was off, had been off for weeks, but there was a cold room with a stone floor that stayed cool in summer, and I put the fish there and we stood in the doorway watching them settle, pressing their flat bodies against the cold stone, arranging themselves in the way flatfish arrange themselves, overlapping, patient, waiting for the light to change so they could go on being fish in water. "Half price," I said. "Full price." "Petra, I've got nothing else to sell you. These are all I've got." "Full price. Because I've been standing in this shop for a month selling nothing, and these are the first fish I've seen that aren't a funeral." She picked one up again. Held it against her chest, where the hum had been strongest, where her molars had felt the pressure. "I'm charging you full price and I'm not letting you argue." I didn't argue. I paid her what the fish were worth, which was more than they were worth, which was more than money meant on Brough now, where the economy had collapsed to the level of a man selling bait to a woman who sold bait, because that was all there was left to sell. Mara was in the kitchen when I got home, sitting at the table with Callum's photo album open again, turning pages slowly. She had a cup of tea that was cold, and she was looking at a photograph of her father, my son, no, my daughter's husband, Callum, standing on this dock with me behind him, both of us grinning, both of us younger, both of us believing that the sea would always be the sea. "Flatfish," I said. "Four of them. Alive. Right-colored." She closed the album. She stood up and came to the window, where the structures sat in the late afternoon light, grey and wide and patient, and she looked at them the way she'd looked at them before, with the calculation of someone deciding whether something was true. "You caught them," she said. "I caught them." "You went out again." "I went out again." She was quiet for a moment. The structures hummed, faintly, that base vibration, that tide-deep pressure, and under it, almost beneath it, something else. Not speech. Not rhythm. Just a faint shaping of sound, like a word being assembled slowly, like a sentence being rehearsed in a language that was still learning what it wanted to say. "I heard something today," she said. "In the shed, with the boxes. It wasn't my mother's voice this time. It was just, a shape. A cadence. Like a question, but I couldn't hear the words." "What did the shape say?" "I don't know. It felt like it was asking me something. Or asking anyone. Or asking the water, through us." I thought about the mackerel, which were gone. The herring, which were gone. The flatfish, which had come back a week early, alive and arguing with the hook. I thought about the translucent thing in the second trap, going deep, going fast, going somewhere that wasn't the mackerel's place but might become the flatfish's place, or the cod's, or some fish that didn't exist yet and would be named by someone who wasn't me. "I think it's rebuilding," I said. "The water. Not replacing it. Rebuilding. Like when they drain a harbor and put in new foundations and let it fill back in with the tide. The fish are going to come back. Different fish, maybe. But the water's being made again." "That's not the same as my mother saying 'come home.'" "No," I said. "That's not the same." She sat back down. She opened the album to the page with the photograph of me and Callum on the dock, grinning, and she looked at it for a while without speaking. The structures hummed. The tea went colder. Outside, the light was going gold behind the structures, making the water look like a road, like a library, like a sea that was being read in a new order. "I'll stay another week," she said. "I need to finish the boxes. And I want to see what comes out of the third trap in September." "You can see from the dock." "I want to be in the kitchen while you're doing it. I want to know when the flatfish come back and stay back." That was fair. That was human. That was a daughter in a kitchen with her father, watching a sea that was broken and healing and still full of things I couldn't name. I went to the shed and checked the nets. They were mended. They were clean. They were ready. I spitted over my left shoulder, and the structures heard it, or didn't, and the hum went on, and the tide went out, and somewhere in the deep water the flatfish pressed themselves against the bottom and waited for the light to change, and I went inside and got the fork from the drawer and ate my dinner properly, with utensils, like a man who believed there would be more dinners to come.

The plan says "No neat ending" and "No cosmic imagery," but this speech is essentially Ren delivering the story's thesis. The chapter follows the plan reasonably well: four flatfish, Petra's shop, the half-price/full-price negotiation (reversed from the plan but effectively so), Mara in the kitchen, the hum returning, Ren going out anyway. Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is a genuinely accomplished piece of speculative fiction that earns most of what it attempts. The narrator, Ren, is a Scottish island fisherman rendered with remarkable specificity and consistency: his habit of spitting over his left shoulder, his preference for cold stew eaten with fingers, his emotional reticence expressed through action rather than declaration. These details accumulate into a believable, lived-in character rather than a type. The central conceit — that the megastructures communicate differently to different listeners, that Ren hears "we are the change in your water," Petra hears "your water owes," and Mara hears her dead mother saying "come home" — is genuinely creative and philosophically interesting. It sidesteps the cliché of alien communication as code-breaking and instead frames it as something more like resonance with individual grief and knowledge. This is the story's strongest invention. The prose style is controlled and distinctive. The narrator's voice is consistent throughout: laconic, observational, occasionally wry. The sentence rhythms feel earned rather than performed. "I spitted over my left shoulder at nothing in particular and went to bed" is a perfect closing beat for a scene. The fish-death sequence in Chapter 1 is particularly well-handled — the mackerel with clear eyes, the wrong weight of dead fish, the gutting out of curiosity — these are specific and strange in the right way. However, there are weaknesses worth examining critically. The metaphors occasionally tip into self-consciousness. "Like a library" appears twice (once from Petra, once echoed by Ren), and the "road leading somewhere" image for the water recurs multiple times. The phrase "the sea that was broken and healing and still full of things I couldn't name" in the final chapter is the kind of sentence that sounds profound but is actually quite vague. Similarly, "the water with more intention than water should have" is used more than once and loses force on repetition. The pacing is uneven. Chapters 1 and 2 are excellent — the slow accumulation of wrongness, the order of dying, the texture of island life disrupted. But Chapters 5 and 6 sag. Chapter 6 in particular, the kitchen sink repair, is a domestic interlude that doesn't quite earn its place. The sink as metaphor for Ren's avoidance is too legible, too neat. The story tells us "Not the leak itself. The evidence of how long I'd let it go" — which is the kind of explanatory gloss that undercuts what should be shown. Mara is the most interesting secondary character but is somewhat underwritten. Her grief for Callum (who is ill, not dead, though the story sometimes treats him as a kind of absence) and her relationship with her father are sketched rather than developed. The revelation that she heard her dead mother's voice is powerful, but the story doesn't fully explore what this means for her — it's processed quickly and moved past. The dialogue is generally strong but occasionally lapses into thesis-statement exchanges. "That's not a communication. That's a manipulation" and "A chord has the same notes for everyone, Dad. The notes don't change based on who's listening" are characters articulating the story's themes rather than speaking naturally. Petra's dialogue is the most convincing throughout. The ending — flatfish returning, Ren eating with a fork — is well-judged. The fork is a small, earned symbol: a man who believes there will be more dinners. This is the kind of quiet, specific gesture that the story does best. The "unearned transformation" question is interesting here. Ren doesn't transform dramatically, which is actually appropriate — he's a man defined by continuity and stubbornness. The flatfish returning is not a resolution but a tentative sign, and the story is honest about this. The structures remain unexplained, which is the right choice. The world-building is effective in its restraint. We get the mainland's bureaucratic response, the survey woman, the pub television, Davie in Inverness — enough to suggest a wider world without losing the island's claustrophobic specificity. One structural weakness: the story is told in retrospect ("A month ago the megastructures arrived") but the narration doesn't consistently feel retrospective. This creates a slight tonal inconsistency that the story never fully resolves. Overall, this is a strong, distinctive piece with a clear authorial voice, genuine creative invention in its central conceit, and mostly earned emotional beats. Its weaknesses are real but not fatal: some metaphor repetition, occasional over-explanation, and a middle section that loses momentum. Model Output:
# Brainstorming The prompt is a text message at midnight: three blood droplet emojis. Darkly comic British YA fiction. Let me cast a wide net. **Character possibilities:** - A teenager who receives the text from an unknown number, terrified it's a threat - A teenager who receives the text from a friend who's in danger - A teenager who receives the text from themselves (accidental send, or... something stranger) - The text could be a misunderstanding: a friend in a horror film, a medical situation (period, injury), a joke gone wrong - A teen who's already been receiving strange messages and this is the culmination - The sender could be a neighbour, a school bully, a parent, a stranger - Setting: rural village in Yorkshire/Dorset, or an inner-city council estate in Manchester/Leeds **Plot directions:** 1. Misunderstanding spirals: The teen panics, tells parents, tells school, tells the police, and the actual cause is something mundane and embarrassing (a friend filming a TikTok about a fake blood spill, a dog vomiting red food dye). The comedy is in the escalation and the public humiliation of the overreaction. 2. Genuine menace with comic deflection: The text IS a warning about something real (a gas leak, a burglar, a fight at the pub), but the teen's response is completely disproportionate. They barricade themselves in, call three different emergency services, narrate everything to their pet cat. 3. Social media paranoia: In an age of creepypasta and doomscrolling, the teen believes this is some viral horror challenge. They investigate online, find nothing, and end up more terrified by the internet than by the actual situation. 4. The sender is dead: Ghost story angle, darkly comic. The teen keeps getting messages from someone who shouldn't be alive. Very British gothic YA. 5. The teen is the sender: They send it to a friend to scare them, and it goes catastrophically wrong. The friend takes it seriously, and now the teen has to manage the fallout while pretending they were joking. 6. Serial texts: The three blood drops are part of a longer message that gets sent piecemeal, or the teen receives multiple escalating texts over the night. **Tone considerations:** - British YA means: understatement, self-deprecating narration, regional speech patterns, references to school life, parents' passive aggression, council flats or village houses, Greggs, bus passes, GCSEs - Darkly comic: The darkness should be present (genuine fear, maybe actual danger) but filtered through absurdity, social awkwardness, and the teen's inability to cope with serious situations - Think: "A Monster Calls" meets "I Am Not Okay With This" meets "The End of the F***ing World" - Avoid: American YA melodrama, tidy moral endings, inspirational speeches **Story beats for 8 chapters (~1000 words each):** - Ch 1: The text arrives. Establish character, setting, midnight atmosphere, immediate panic - Ch 2: First response, telling a friend, the friend's inadequate reaction, escalation begins - Ch 3: The investigation phase, checking phones, checking social media, the rational mind trying to work while the irrational mind spirals - Ch 4: Telling an adult, parental reaction, more comedy of misunderstanding - Ch 5: The truth starts to emerge or the situation worsens, the teen is stuck between two versions of reality - Ch 6: Confrontation or discovery - Ch 7: The actual resolution, whatever the blood drops meant - Ch 8: Aftermath, changed but not redeemed, British-style ending (slightly unresolved, wry) **Specific character idea:** - Name: something very British YA, Maeve, Callum, Isla, Rory. Let's say: **Joss**, 16, lives in a semi-detached in South Yorkshire or somewhere similar - Best friend: **Dre** (Drewe?), 17, calm to a fault, possibly the actual sender or the one who can decode the situation - Parent: **Mum**, practical, tired, makes everything about dinner or bills - The sender: ambiguous until late in the story **Alternative: The blood drops are a code.** In the story, it turns out the teen's missing sibling/friend is using it as a check-in signal, "I'm alive, I've been hurt, help me." This gives genuine stakes under the comedy. **Another alternative:** The teen is a blood donor (or has a condition like ITP or is in a hospital) and the text is from a hospital system confirming something routine. The whole night is a false alarm built on a teen's fear of their own body. # Reflection The pure misunderstanding angle (option 1) is the safest comic route but risks being too neat, teen panics, it was nothing, everyone laughs. Too tidy. The social media paranoia angle (option 3) feels most authentically contemporary YA. Teens do actually do this, Google everything, find worse information, spiral. But it could drag across 8 chapters if it's all just "she looked at her phone." The dead sender (option 4) leans supernatural, less comic, more gothic. Could work but drifts from "darkly comic" toward "darkly creepy." I like the combination: The blood drops are a genuine but small injury (friend cut her hand on a jam jar, friend had a nosebleed, friend scraped her elbow on a kerb), sent at the wrong time by the wrong phone, or sent as a joke that landed wrong. The comedy comes from the gap between the actual event and the teen's catastrophic interpretation. But I want genuine darkness threaded through, the teen should have a real reason to be anxious, maybe she's recently lost someone, or has health anxiety, or there's a missing person in the local news. The darkness isn't the blood drops; it's the fact that the teen reads them through a lens of her own unresolved fear. The strongest structure: Joss receives the text from Dre's number. Dre is her best friend. Dre doesn't answer her calls. The night is spent in Joss's room, on the cold Yorkshire hillside, with the window open and the dog asleep downstairs, Joss constructing increasingly elaborate narratives about what happened to Dre. Mum is asleep. There's a power cut. The neighbours' dogs are barking. Every ordinary thing becomes evidence of catastrophe. By morning Dre shows up with a bloody bandaged finger and a very flat explanation. But I want the ending to not be purely "it was nothing." Maybe Joss learns something about Dre while investigating, or maybe the text wasn't from Dre at all, it was from a random number, which is worse, which means the story doesn't end with a tidy bow. Actually, the darkest comic version: it was from a random number. Nobody knows why. Dre wasn't the sender. The story ends with Joss still unsure, and the reader unsure, and that's the British way, don't resolve the horror, just resolve the breakfast. Chapters: 8 x ~1000 words = 8000 words total. Tight. Each chapter needs one clear beat. I'll aim for escalation of paranoia with comic deflections at each step, then the ambiguous ending.

Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>

# Intention The story will centre on Joss, 16, in a semi-detached house in the Pennines, who receives "🩸🩸🩸" from an unknown number at 12:04am on a Saturday. The comedy comes from the escalating gap between her catastrophic interpretations and the mundane world pressing in around her: Mum calling down to ask if she's eaten, the dog knocking her leg over, the power cutting out, the neighbour's drunk argument. The darkness comes from Joss's underlying anxiety, her sister left home six months ago and has stopped answering texts, and so Joss reads any sign of trouble as proof of the same fate arriving for her own people. Voice: first person, past tense, present-minded. Joss narrates with the breathlessness of panic but also with the deadpan British habit of understating everything ("It was fine. I was fine. It was not fine."). Short paragraphs. Occasional italicised internal commentary. No tidy moral. What I am avoiding: the friend-shows-up-and-it-was-a-joke ending. I want the text to remain unexplained. Dre is a red herring. The sender is never identified. The story ends with Joss having spent a night in her bedroom becoming a person who now checks her phone differently, who flinches at unknown numbers, and who has decided not to tell anyone how badly she shook at 4am. British YA ends with a feeling, not a resolution. What I am aiming for: genuine physical detail (the smell of the cold room, the battery percentage dropping, the sound of the neighbour's bin lid banging), comic deflection from adults who treat midnight emergencies as dinner questions, and the slow creep of the reader's own uncertainty. Is this a thriller or a story about a girl in bed too late? Both. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 (approx 1000 words):** Joss is awake at midnight because she's been doomscrolling about her sister's silence. The text arrives. She checks the number: unsaved. She reads it three times. The immediate physical panic, cold fingers, phone held like it might bite. She decides it's a prank or a wrong number and goes to sleep. But sleep doesn't come. Ends with her watching the number glow on her lock screen. **Chapter 2 (approx 1000 words):** She messages Dre, no reply. She messages her sister, no reply. Panic compounds. She searches the number online: nothing. She finds a thread about blood-drop texts being a "viral dare" where someone texts a friend and they have to send back their location or "something happens." Joss decides this is real. She starts Googling local missing person reports. The neighbour's dog starts howling. **Chapter 3 (approx 1000 words):** She wakes Mum. Mum's reaction is entirely about the heating and whether Joss wants toast before she goes back to sleep. Mum thinks it's a prank. Joss can't explain why she can't explain it. Mum's phone buzzes with a text from her own sister asking about the school run, a mundane intrusion that Joss finds offensive in its normality. She goes back to her room. The power cuts out. **Chapter 4 (approx 1000 words):** The dark. The cold. Joss barricades her door for reasons she cannot articulate. She calls the police. A bored operator tells her to call back if anyone actually comes in. She calls the police again, a different voice. They ask if she's safe. She says yes. She says yes again. The dog is under the stairs growling at nothing. She starts writing down everything she has seen, heard, smelled, like a witness. **Chapter 5 (approx 1000 words):** Morning approaches. She has been up since midnight and has done nothing but sit with her phone. She considers going downstairs, making tea, doing something normal. Instead she checks her sister's social media, last post three weeks ago, a photo of a kitchen that doesn't match where her sister lives. Paranoia now has texture and specifics. Her sister is lying about something, or her sister is gone, or Joss is losing it. **Chapter 6 (approx 1000 words):** Dre calls at 8:17am. Voice groggy, confused. "Why are you texting me? You've been sending me like nine messages." Joss realises Dre never got the blood drops. The text wasn't from Dre. It wasn't from anyone Joss knows. The silence after the call is worse than the noise before it. She asks Dre if anyone at school knows anything. Nobody does. **Chapter 7 (approx 1000 words):** Joss decides not to tell Mum. She eats cereal standing in the kitchen doorway, watching the garden where nothing is happening, which is the thing she now cannot tolerate. She thinks about what it would mean if the text were real: someone knows where she lives, someone knows her phone number, someone wants her to feel unsafe. Or: it was a bot. A glitch. A stranger with a bored thumb. She writes a text to the unknown number: "WHO ARE YOU?" and does not send it. She does not send it. **Chapter 8 (approx 1000 words):** School. The day is ordinary in its terrible way, Maths, Greggs, someone's boyfriend problem. But Joss is different. She keeps her phone face-down on the desk. She sits near the door. When a new girl asks for the time, Joss gives it and doesn't notice she's checked the sender ID of the incoming call twice. Evening: she texts her sister again. No reply. But at 11:58pm, before the unknown number could send anything, a message comes from her sister: "Sorry love. Been bad week. Love you too." Joss sits with this. Then she checks her inbox for the unknown number. Empty. The blood drops are gone or they were never there. She locks her phone. She lies in the dark, breathing, and doesn't sleep.

# Human Approach vs LLM Approach ## Telltale LLM writing habits and why they'd wreck this piece **The tidy arc.** LLMs love a clean emotional trajectory: panic → escalation → discovery → resolution → changed character. A human writer of darkly comic British YA would resist this. Joss should not be "changed" in a legible way. She should be the same girl at the end who is slightly different, in ways she can't even articulate, maybe she just holds her phone differently now, maybe she still texts her sister every night and counts the seconds until a reply. The plan's ending does this partially, but the sister's reply at the end is still too neat. It's a gift. A human writer would be crueler: the sister never replies. Or the sister replies at 2am with "u ok?" and no explanation, which is worse. **Over-explained panic.** LLMs tend to narrate every beat of emotion: "My heart hammered. My breath caught. I couldn't move." A human would show it through action: Joss bites her thumbnail until it stings, rearranges her charger cables on the desk, checks her phone so many times the screen goes dim. Panic in a 16-year-old is not a Shakespearean crisis; it's the inability to get to sleep and the sudden horror of the ceiling. **The "deeply meaningful" moment.** LLMs reach for gravitas at the wrong moments. A human British YA writer would keep things flat. When Joss barricades her door, it should be described with the same register as making a sandwich, because from the inside, that's how it feels. The comedy is in the equivalence of scale. "I wedged the chair under the handle, the way you'd wedge a door to keep out the dog, except I didn't have a dog to keep out, and the thing outside wasn't a dog." **Melodrama of the setting.** LLMs love to make the storm outside mirror the inner storm. The power cut is borderline cliché here. A human might keep it, but would use it differently: not as atmosphere but as practical inconvenience. Joss's phone battery drops to 14% and now the real enemy is that she can't check whether anyone else has messaged her. The horror is logistical. **Symmetry and neat callbacks.** LLMs bookend stories. Chapter 1: she checks the number. Chapter 8: she checks the number again. A human might do this, but would also do things that don't mirror. Chapter 4 has the power cut; Chapter 6 has Dre calling at 8:17am, and the specific oddness of the time is the point, not the symmetry of dawn. **Moralising.** LLMs love to let the character state the lesson learned. "I learned that fear makes you see things that aren't there." Never. Joss should not learn anything. She should just be a girl who now checks unknown senders before answering texts, and who finds that habit slightly sad in daylight. **The wise adult.** Mum should not be a foil who says one calm line and fixes the emotional weather. A human would give Mum three different mundane concerns and make Joss's irritation at her mother part of the darkness, the fact that no one believes her is itself the loneliness. Mum isn't wise; Mum is tired and hungry and thinks Joss is being dramatic, and Joss can't blame her entirely, which is the worst part. ## Specific critique of the current plan **The sister subplot.** This is the weakest part. It's the standard "underlying darkness" device: character has an unresolved trauma that explains their fear. It works, but it's the thing an LLM would reach for to add depth. A human might instead make the darkness more immediate and less biographical: Joss is afraid not because of her sister's history but because of something in the news this week, a girl in the village whose phone went silent and she was found three days later in a drainage ditch. Real, local, recent. The horror has a place and a date. That's scarier and more British than a vague "sister left home" backstory. **The power cut.** Keep it but reframe. The power cut is not atmospheric; it's the thing that forces Joss to be alone with her phone and her thoughts in a way that daylight prevents. Without electricity, there's no TV in the living room to provide background noise. The silence is the enemy. **The police call.** This could be too tidy. An LLM would have the operator dismiss her, which is comic but expected. A human might make it weirder: the operator is kind, genuinely kind, and asks her if she's been drinking, and Joss, who is sixteen and hasn't touched alcohol, feels accused in a way that shames her for being afraid. The comedy is in the kindness being worse than the dismissal. **The Greggs mention.** One reference to Greggs in Chapter 8 is fine, but LLMs love British YA name-checking: Greggs, council flats, "innit," passive aggression about homework. A human would use one or two and then stop. The Britishness should be in the behaviour (understatement, politeness under duress, the specific awkwardness of asking a stranger a serious question), not in a vocabulary list. **The unknown number never being identified.** This is good and I'd keep it, but a human might add one small wrong turn: Joss finds a forum post where someone else received blood-drop texts, and the replies are a mixture of "it's a bot" and "my friend got these and then she disappeared" and one person who says "I think it's a spam campaign." The mundane explanation is always one comment away. **The final sister message.** As noted, too neat. Alternative: Joss texts her sister at the end and there's a "seen" tick, no reply. Or better: no contact at all, and the chapter ends with Joss putting her phone in her pocket and going outside for air, and the darkness being the actual Yorkshire darkness, the fields, the nothingness of the landscape, which is how the place always was and is not now a threat. **What's genuinely human to add:** - Joss makes a sandwich she doesn't eat, just to have something to do with her hands - She counts the tiles in the bathroom ceiling because it's an old anxiety technique - The specific shame of being sixteen and unable to explain why she can't sleep - Dre's voice sounding stupidly normal, "you've been sending me nine messages" as if that's a small thing, and Joss almost crying at the ordinariness of it - The battery percentage as a countdown she can't control - She writes "WHO ARE YOU?" and doesn't send it, but she also doesn't delete it, and it sits there in drafts, which is the most adult thing she does all night ## What a human would probably do differently with structure A human might not give each chapter a clean emotional beat. Chapter 3 could be mostly dialogue with Mum, comic and deflating. Chapter 5 could be mostly interiority, no new information, just Joss sitting with what she knows. A human trusts the reader to follow a slow chapter. LLMs pad slow chapters with action because they assume boredom. A human might also let Joss be a little unsympathetic. She's dramatic. She knows it's probably nothing. She does it anyway. The reader should partly judge her, which makes the ending land differently when the text remains unexplained: was she right to be afraid? The story shouldn't answer that.

Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>

The text is never explained. That is the point. Voice: first person, past tense. Concrete physical detail (battery percentages, ceiling tiles, the smell of the dog). No italics for emphasis, except maybe twice, because a real sixteen-year-old would italicise twice. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc

# Joss (Josephine) Marsh **Background:** Sixteen. Lives in a semi-detached house on a cul-de-sac in a town just off the A61 in South Yorkshire. Her dad left when she was eleven, not dramatically, just a gradual fading out of the house until there was no one home at night to be left. Mum works weekends at a pharmacy chain. Joss is in Year 11, GCSEs done, A-levels in English, History, and PE because she thought PE was easier than Geography. She's average at English, decent at History, good at PE but hates the sport itself. She reads a lot, mostly the kind of books with dead people in them. **Personality:** Joss presents as calm. She is the friend people come to when they're sad because she nods and doesn't offer advice. Underneath she is catastrophising at a constant, low hum. She reads news reports like they're about her personally. She has a folder on her phone called "things to check" that contains a list of things she's worried about, carbon monoxide alarm batteries, the date of the last time she saw her sister, whether the new boy at school is watching her or just looking past her. **Flaws:** She cannot say "I'm frightened" out loud to a human being. She will say "I'm not great" or "it's a bit weird." She overthinks adult interactions until they lose meaning. She also has a mean streak she's ashamed of, she can be cruel to people who are vulnerable, once told a girl at lunch she looked like a "wet cat" and felt guilty for three days and did it again to someone else a month later. **Idiosyncracies:** Bites her thumbnail on her right index finger until it's just the pink of it. Makes sandwiches she doesn't eat. Counts ceiling tiles when she can't sleep. Has a playlist called "for when I need to not be here" that is entirely songs she doesn't like, because the not-liking is the point. Wears the same oversized grey jumper every day in winter. **Physicality:** Five foot two. Thin in the way of someone who forgets to eat when her brain is doing something. Dark hair usually tied back with a claw clip that's gone missing on one side. Brown eyes that look tired most of the time. Carries herself slightly hunched, shoulders in, like she's trying to take up less space. When she's really anxious she touches her phone to her chest like it's a talisman. **Motives:** She wants to understand the text. More than that, she wants to be able to explain it away to herself, because if she can't explain it away then the world is full of unknown numbers sending things at midnight and there is no safety in it. She also wants her sister to be fine, which is a want she can't quite name because her sister is fine, probably, and Joss knows that, which doesn't stop the want. **Relationships:** Mum, practical, tired, loving in the way of someone who expresses care through food and practical questions. Dre, best friend since secondary school, the calm one, the one who talks people down. Her sister, Callum, twenty, went to Leeds to do an art degree and then stopped answering texts. Joss has decided this means either Callum is depressed or Callum is in trouble, and she has no evidence for either and will not accept a third option. **Voice:** "I wasn't crying. There was just a thing in my throat that I couldn't get rid of and I wasn't going to explain that to anyone." "The thing about panic is it makes you want to do something useful. I kept thinking if I just, if I just did one sensible thing, it would sort of organise the whole thing." # Drewe (Dre) Okafor **Background:** Seventeen. Lives three streets away, also semi-detached, also South Yorkshire. In Year 12, A-levels in Maths, Physics, and Music. Joss met him in Year 9 when he sat next to her in a corridor and said she looked like she was having a mental breakdown, which she was, and they've been friends since. He's Nigerian-British; his parents moved here from Birmingham for work. He's the only one of their group who actually does homework. **Personality:** Dre is calm to the point of being annoying. He is not unfeeling; he simply has a way of arriving at the practical solution before the emotional response can fully form. If Joss panics, Dre says "okay" and asks what happened. If Joss rants, Dre listens and then says "and?" as if the rant were a premise he needs a conclusion for. He has a dry, low sense of humour. He doesn't raise his voice even when he's angry, which is scarier than raising it. **Flaws:** He underestimates how much his calm can hurt. He says "probably nothing" and means it, but Joss hears "you're being ridiculous." He also sometimes forgets that people need to feel heard before they need to be helped. He will solve the problem while the person is still describing it. **Idiosyncracies:** Texts with one word at a time, "ok" then "what" then "happened," like he's assembling sentences out of Lego. Wears the same headphones on his neck even when not using them. Has a habit of tilting his head when listening, as if physically trying to hear more clearly. Keeps a battered copy of *A Brief History of Time* in his bag "for the jokes." **Physicality:** Five foot nine. Medium build, broad shoulders from playing football at the park. Dark skin, short natural hair that his mum keeps trying to cut with scissors. Dresses like everything is optional: hoodies, trainers that are scuffed. Moves slowly, unhurried. When he talks to Joss he tends to stand with his hands in his pockets and look at the ground slightly, not dismissively, just habitually. **Motives:** He wants Joss to be okay because she's his friend and her panic is contagious in a way he can't handle. He also wants to get home and finish his physics revision, which he is not ashamed to admit. He has no investment in the unknown number. From his perspective, Joss has been awake since midnight doing nothing useful, and he doesn't understand why. **Relationships:** Joss is his closest friend, and he worries about her in the way of someone who finds worry inefficient. His parents are warm but busy; his older sister is in London and sends photos of herself that Dre likes but never comments on. **Voice:** "You've been awake since midnight doing what, exactly? Because if the answer is staring at your phone, then the phone is the problem, not the number." "Okay. That's fine. So you're not in danger. Cool. Can we go to Greggs or are you still going to be on the floor?" # Mum (Margaret Marsh) **Background:** Forty-six. Works weekends and weekday mornings at a pharmacy chain, which means she is home in the afternoons but often tired when Joss comes back from school. Single mother since Joss's dad faded out, which she talks about in a single flat sentence when necessary: "Your dad's in Manchester now." No elaboration. She has a sister in Leeds she's close with. She does the school run in a car with a cracked windscreen she has been meaning to fix for two years. **Personality:** Practical to the point of being almost robotic about emotions. She does not ask "how are you feeling?" She asks "have you eaten?" and "do you need anything from the shops?" Her love language is logistics. She is not cruel; she is genuinely bad at processing other people's fear, and she covers this with busyness and food. If Joss came to her crying about a ghost, Mum would probably offer her a biscuit and ask if she'd locked the back door. **Flaws:** She reads emotional distress as drama. Not because she doesn't care, but because her own life has taught her that most things people panic about resolve themselves by morning. She also has a habit of changing the subject when a conversation becomes heavy, deflecting with a question about food or the weather or the washing. **Idiosyncracies:** Always smells like hand sanitiser and the particular sweetness of the pharmacy's employee tea. Wears her hair in a low bun with a section that always falls out. Keeps a notebook of reminders on the fridge: bills, dates, the name of the school dinner menu. Once said "I'm not being dramatic" while saying something extremely dramatic. **Physicality:** Five foot six. Solid build, not heavy but not light. Dresses in practical terms: jeans, jumpers, boots for the cold. Hands are rough from work. Moves with purpose, always heading somewhere, always doing something with her hands while she talks. **Motives:** She wants Joss to be safe and fed and to get to sleep. She is tired. She has been working since five this morning at the pharmacy and she wants to understand why her daughter is frightened of a text message, but she is also afraid of how that answer might feel to give. **Voice:** "Have you eaten? Because you look like you haven't and it's nearly eight." "It's probably a wrong number, love. People send messages to wrong numbers all the time. It's not like it's the first text you've ever gotten that you didn't recognise."

The map app showed the last known location as a petrol station on the Ring Road, which was a forty-minute drive from her house, so she could almost see it. Not really, but in her head she could see the forecourt and the chip shop behind it and the specific slant of the lights at 3am when the news said she'd been last seen. Joss closed the app. Opened it again. Closed it. She'd been awake for two hours doing this, which was stupid, because nothing was going to happen to the missing girl's memory by the fact of Joss's attention. But her brain had a system for this, a little loop where it took a sad story and turned it into a question, and the question was always *what if*, and the answer was always *you can't know*, and *you can't know* was not an answer her brain accepted. The phone buzzed at 12:04am. She looked at it without picking it up because she was lying on her front, her cheek against the duvet, her phone balanced on her sternum. The notification was grey and small. Unknown sender. The preview showed three emojis, and the preview was the only thing she could see because she hadn't unlocked the screen yet. Three blood drops. 🩸🩸🩸 She picked up the phone. Held it at arm's length, as if it were a phone that could burn her. The number was +44 followed by digits she didn't recognise, not local, not a number that belonged to anyone she knew. The sender ID just said Unknown. *Spam*, said the part of her brain that was tired and wanted sleep. *Or a prank. Or someone testing their phone. Or a bot that's gone wrong, the way the bank sent you a message last month about your overdraft in a way that made your stomach do that thing.* She read the text again. Three drops. Nothing else. No words, no question, no "are you there", no laughing emoji to soften it. Just the blood, repeated, patient. She checked the time. 12:04. She checked her contacts. Dre's name. Callum's name. Her mum's name. All the people she might have been talking to before midnight if she hadn't been sitting here reading about a girl who had stopped answering texts. Joss typed: *Did you send me something?* She sent it to Dre. Then she sent it to Callum. Then she sat on her bed with her hands around the phone and waited, and the phone did not reply, because Dre was asleep and Callum had not replied to anything in three weeks, and the unknown number just sat there in her inbox like a small red stain. The room was cold. She could see her breath if she looked up at the window, which she didn't, because the window had nothing to do with this, it was just a window in a house on a cul-de-sac in the dark, the way all windows were on cold nights, and she was sixteen and not a person who needed to see her own breath to understand that the outside was outside. The dog downstairs shifted. A soft sound, like a blanket being dragged across linoleum. *You're being ridiculous,* she told herself. *You're being stupid and old. This is a text message. Someone pressed three emojis on their phone and it went somewhere. It went here. You could call them. You could ask. You could do the one sensible thing and just, text them back and say "who are you", and then it would be a thing with an explanation, and then you could sleep.* She opened a new message. Started typing. *WHO ARE YOU?* She stared at it. The caps made it look like shouting. The question mark made it look like she was accusing someone of something. She deleted the message. Instead she wrote: *hi* Sent it to the unknown number. No reply. Obviously. Of course not. She was sixteen and she had just sent the word "hi" to a stranger at midnight and expected, what, a response? A friendship? An explanation? But the not-responding was its own kind of answer. It said: I am here. I sent you something. And I am not talking to you now. She put the phone face-down on her duvet. Turned her head to the side. The screen went dark, then dimmed further, then nothing, and the room was just a room again, dark and cold and ordinary, with the duvet smell and the window gap where the draft lived and the ceiling above her that she could count tiles on if she wanted to, though she couldn't see them. She counted them anyway. From memory. From the version of the ceiling that existed in her head. Fourteen across. Nine down. She counted to the end and started again, because the counting was a thing she did when her brain was doing too much and the counting didn't make it stop but it gave her hands something else to do. The dog barked once, low, at the garden. At nothing. At the dark where nothing was. She lay still. Somewhere in the back of her mind, behind the panic and the stupid questions, there was the other thing, the thing she'd been doing all night, the thing the text had made worse because it was proof, not proof of anything real, but proof of the pattern: people's phones go silent, and then they're gone, and their mum calls the police and the police say *last seen at the petrol station* and the world does not slow down for it. Callum's name was still grey in her messages. Three weeks. The last text had been "sorry love been busy" and Joss had replied "u ok?" and there had been a *seen* tick and then nothing. *Seen.* She closed her eyes. The phone was face-down on her duvet, two feet from her hand, and if she reached for it she would see the unknown number glowing there, three blood drops, patient, waiting, and she would have to decide what it meant, and the not-deciding was the only thing that felt like safety right now. She didn't reach for it. The dog stopped barking. The wind moved the window frame a little, the specific sound of a house settling into the cold. Somewhere far away a lorry went past, low and long, like a held breath released. Joss lay on her front in the dark and tried to be a person whose phone was quiet and whose sister had replied and whose neighbourhood was just a neighbourhood, not a place where girls walked away from a petrol station at 3am and never walked back. It didn't work. At 12:31 she checked the messages anyway. No replies. Nothing new. The blood drops still there, red and small, like three wounds she'd made on the inside of her own phone screen.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a genuinely accomplished piece of YA fiction that largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me work through its strengths and weaknesses carefully. **Voice and Character** The voice is the chapter's greatest achievement. Joss's narration has the flat, catastrophising register the plan promised: "She'd been awake for two hours doing this, which was stupid, because nothing was going to happen to the missing girl's memory by the fact of Joss's attention." This is exactly right — the self-awareness that doesn't stop the behaviour, the slightly formal internal phrasing that a reader who overthinks would use. The detail of sending "hi" to the unknown number and then immediately recognising the absurdity of expecting a response is psychologically precise and quietly funny in the way the plan intended. The physical details are well-chosen and specific without being showy: the phone balanced on her sternum, the draft in the window frame, the dog's sound described as "a blanket being dragged across linoleum." These ground the piece in a real, cold, unglamorous Yorkshire night. **The Callum Thread** The sister subplot is handled with exactly the restraint the plan called for. The "seen" tick that arrived and meant nothing is devastating in its understatement. The plan said "no backstory speech, no dramatic reveal" and the chapter honours this — Callum exists as a grey name in a message thread, and that's enough. **Weaknesses and Concerns** The chapter has some moments where the prose reaches slightly too hard. "Like three wounds she'd made on the inside of her own phone screen" is the closing line, and it's the chapter's most strained metaphor — it's trying to be resonant but the logic doesn't quite hold (she didn't make the wounds; the unknown sender did, and the "inside of her own phone screen" is a slightly confused spatial image). The plan specifically warned against over-explained panic and atmospheric mirroring, and this closing line edges toward the latter. "Like a small red stain" for the unknown number sitting in her inbox is similarly reaching — it's not bad, but it's the kind of image that announces itself as literary in a way that slightly undercuts the flat register the rest of the chapter maintains. The lorry simile — "low and long, like a held breath released" — is the chapter's most questionable poetic leap. A lorry going past doesn't really sound like a held breath released; it's an associative connection that doesn't survive scrutiny. This is exactly the kind of "poetic riffing" that should be penalised when it doesn't land. **Plot and Plan Adherence** The chapter follows its plan closely: the map app doomscrolling, the text arriving at 12:04, the unknown number, texting Dre and Callum, putting the phone face-down, the dog barking. The plan mentioned she "sleeps badly" and "the number glows through the cover" — the chapter doesn't quite deliver the glowing-through-cover image, and Joss doesn't really sleep at all in this chapter, which is a minor deviation. The chapter ends at 12:31 with her checking messages, which is consistent with the plan's implication of a bad night. **Dialogue** There is essentially no dialogue in this chapter, which is appropriate — it's a solitary midnight scene. The internal monologue functions as the chapter's "voice" and it's well-handled. **Darkness and Comedy** The darkly comic register is present but light in this chapter — appropriately so, since this is the setup chapter. The comedy of sending "hi" to a stranger at midnight is the clearest instance. The darkness is well-earned through the Callum thread and the missing girl context. **Overall Assessment** This is a strong opening chapter that mostly earns its effects. The voice is distinctive and consistent, the psychological realism is good, and the restraint around the sister subplot is admirable. The main weaknesses are two or three metaphors that reach beyond what the prose can support, and a closing line that tries slightly too hard. These are real flaws but not fatal ones — the chapter is substantially better than average YA fiction and shows genuine craft. Morning came the way mornings do in the Pennines, not with brightness but with a grey that was lighter than the dark. Joss was awake when it started, which meant she hadn't slept, and she knew she hadn't slept because she remembered every minute of the night. The counting. The phone. The dog. The way she'd held her breath for a long time while the neighbour's argument downstairs ended with a door slammed so hard the house shuddered. Her phone was at 31%. She didn't reach for it. Instead she sat up, pushed the duvet off, and put her feet on the cold floor. The floor was the right temperature, which was the only temperature she could tolerate, so that was fine. She got her laptop. Opened it. Typed the unknown number into the search bar with the +44 in front, because she'd read somewhere that searching with the country code sometimes got better results, though "sometimes" was doing a lot of work in that sentence. Nothing. No results. No social profiles. No spam lists. The number existed only as the thing she'd typed, a string of digits that the internet had never heard of. She searched the number without the +44. Nothing. She searched the number and the word "text". Nothing. She searched the number and the word "missing". She closed the laptop before she saw what that might return, and then, because she was Joss, opened it again. The search returned a forum thread. The thread was old, two years, but it was about blood-drop texts. Someone had posted: *got a text from unknown number, three blood emojis, anyone know what this means.* The replies were forty-three strong. Joss read them the way she read everything now, looking for the one that matched. Most said *spam.* Some said *bot.* A few said *wrong number.* One person, a username called KiteRunner88, wrote: *My friend got these. She ignored it. Then she stopped picking up her phone for a while. Then she moved away and didn't say goodbye. I don't know what that means either.* Joss read that reply three times. Then there was another reply, below it, from a username that was just the word "sensible": *It's a campaign. People are doing it as a joke. They text a friend and if the friend doesn't reply in an hour, they text more. It's a dare thing. It's stupid. It's not a threat.* *It's stupid*, the reply said. *It's not a threat.* Joss closed the laptop. She was shaking. Not much, not in the way that shows, but enough that she had to hold her hands in her lap where no one could see. She needed to do something. Anything that wasn't sitting in her bedroom reading the internet about dead girls and red emojis. She went downstairs. The kitchen was cold and smelled of the dog, which was the smell of dog food and the plastic bin bags behind the fridge. Mum was at the counter with the kettle, dressed in a top and bottoms, hair still unbrushed, the bun loose at the back. "Morning," Mum said. "Morning." Mum poured milk into a bowl. The dog came in from under the stairs, tail going, and licked Mum's wrist while she fed him. Joss watched this, a girl and a dog and a bowl of milk, and thought: *this is what a Saturday morning looks like when nobody is afraid of anything.* She sat down at the table. Opened her phone. The battery read 28%. "Mum," she said. "Did you get any weird texts last night?" Mum poured the cereal. "Weird how?" "I don't know. Anything from an unknown number." Mum considered this while she measured out the flakes. "Probably. I get a few. The bank sends me things at odd hours, you know." She set the bowl in front of Joss, though Joss hadn't asked for one. "Have you had your breakfast?" Joss looked at the cereal. The cereal looked like a small grey lake. "I want to tell you about something," Joss said. "Go on." "The text came from an unknown number. And it was just, three blood drops. Just the emoji. Nothing else. And it was at midnight." Mum looked at her. Then at the cereal. Then at the dog, who was licking the table. "That's a bit weird," Mum said. "But it's probably nothing. People send all sorts. Remember when your friend got a text from some number saying she owed them money?" "I didn't get a text saying I owe money." "No. But the point is, wrong numbers happen. Spam happens. It's not like it's the first unknown text you've ever gotten." Joss wanted to say: *But this one is different. This one came when I was already looking at a map of where a missing girl was last seen. This one came at the same time I'd been wondering whether my own sister was going to text me back today.* But what came out was: "Yeah." "You should probably ignore it," Mum said. "If it's a prank, ignoring it's the best response. If it's spam, blocking is better." "Okay." "And eat your cereal. You look thin." Joss ate the cereal. It was cold and tasted like the bowl it had been poured from. She chewed through four spoonfuls and then stopped, because her stomach had closed around the idea of food, which was something it did when her brain was running too fast. Mum went back to the sink. Started doing the dishes. The sound of water and the clink of the dog's bowl. The sound of a morning being assembled from ordinary parts. Joss put her phone face-down on the table. She watched Mum's back while she dried a plate. She thought: *if something happens to someone, the first sign is usually small. A text. A silence. A thing that's easy to ignore, because the alternative is admitting you're afraid, and no one wants that, least of all a girl who eats cereal and feeds the dog.* The neighbour's bin lid banged against the fence in the wind. A long, hollow sound, like knocking on a door that wasn't going to open. Joss got up. Left the cereal. Went back upstairs. She didn't tell Mum about the missing girl. She didn't tell her about Callum's three-week silence. She didn't tell her that she'd been awake all night counting ceiling tiles and writing "WHO ARE YOU" and deleting it. She told her she was tired and going back to bed. Mum said "right, love, make sure the heating's on." The heating was on. The heating had been on all night. The house was warm now and the window didn't fog when she breathed and the light through the curtains was the colour of old paper, and the phone on her duvet was quiet, and the blood drops were under the screen, waiting, patient, three small wounds that meant nothing to anyone except the girl lying on her front in the grey morning, unable to close her eyes because closing her eyes made the dark bigger and the dark was where the unknown numbers lived.
