The frost had come in the night, not as a gentle rime but as a hard skin over everything, the garden glass, the trellis oak, the stone lip where Ada placed her heel. She climbed up with the care of a person who knew that the previous night's rain had frozen into a treachery that no amount of ivy-greeting could remedy. She made it three-quarters of the way. Then her left boot found the ice-crusted rail and went nowhere. The world tilted. She dropped her weight back onto the trellis, hung by her right hand, and felt the frost press the stone against her calf like a cold hand. Below her was the garden wall, the lane, the village, and all the people in it who would see her fall and have opinions. A hand caught her wrist. It was not gentle. It was the grip of a man whose hands had never climbed anything, who was holding on with the desperate overcorrection of someone who had just watched a person about to be killed by ice and was responding with everything he had. Ada swung slightly in his grip, the rail grinding under her boot, and she did not have time to be frightened before she was furious. "Let go," she said, and meant it as a command. He did not let go. He pulled her up, which was the wrong thing to do, she would have told him later, because it loaded her elbow joint in a way that would ache for days, but he pulled her up and over the sill and into the room and the sash slammed shut behind her and the cold sealed out like a door. She stood in the companion's room, shaking water off her coat, and glared at him. He was tall. That was the first thing she registered, and then she registered that he was young, and then that he was holding her wrist still, and then that his face had the look of a man who had been waiting and was surprised to be surprised. He was fair, with hair worn long and pushed back with his fingers, and he wore his mother's spectacles, she could see the slight bow of the frames, the particular way he held them as though they were borrowed, because they were. "Sir," she said. "Eleanor," he said, and stopped. He looked at her as though he were reading a word he did not recognize. Then he let go of her wrist and stepped back, which was more than he owed her. "You've been leaving the window open," she said. "I have not been leaving anything. It's been stuck." "It was stuck open exactly a half-inch, which is the width of a deliberate decision." She pulled the coin from her teeth, which she had not realized she was still holding, and set it on the desk between them like a piece of evidence. "You've been watching." He looked at the coin. He looked at the rain-damaged coat, the boot with the twine, the journal still folded inside her collar where it had been all night. "I've been hearing the trellis," he said. "For three nights." "And instead of calling the constabulary you made tea." "I made tea for the house." "You made tea for the window." He had the grace to look uncomfortable, which Ada appreciated because discomfort was honest and she had learned, in her years, that comfort in the presence of an intruder was usually a prelude to something worse. He turned and went to the fire, which was banked low but lit, and pushed a chair toward the sill with his heel. He did not offer it. He simply made it available, the way a person might move an obstacle out of a path. Ada did not sit. She stood at the window, below his eye level, because standing made her feel more equal and sitting made her feel like a guest, and she was not a guest. She was a woman with a debt and a mother's handwriting in a leather cover. "My mother was your mother's companion," she said. "I know." "She wrote to me about the roses and the cat and a cat was not in this room. There is a glass jar of lavender." "Beatrice liked lavender." "Fourteen pounds," she said. "Owed to Mr. Tallow in Marlow. My mother's wages were underpaid here, and she left before the account was settled, and the village now expects me to answer it because I have her name and she does not." Edmund Hale looked at her for a moment with an expression she could not classify. It was not the expression of a man deciding whether to turn her over to Fenwick. It was the expression of a man reading a page in a book he had not expected to find. "Fourteen pounds," he repeated. "I'll look at the ledger." "You've been watching me climb into your house and your first offer is a ledger." He looked away from her, toward the window, toward the trellis where the frost made the oak look silver and treacherous. "I've been in this house six months," he said, and the words came out flat, factual, stripped of the melodrama she might have expected. "I don't know how to have people in it. The tea was, the tea was my mother's habit. I did not choose to do it. My hands did." Ada considered this. She was good at considering. It was one of the few skills the world had given her along with short stature and ruined boots. "I need the pages that detail the wages," she said. "The remaining entries. They're not in the journal, they're in the household accounts, filed by whoever came after her." "I'll find them." "And then I'll settle the debt and I won't climb through your window again." "And if I find the pages and you settle the debt and you don't climb through my window again, the house will be empty again, and I will be in it, and Fenwick will be on the grounds, and the trellis will be thin, and the lavender will go to seed, and, " He stopped. He looked at her. "You're short." It was not a compliment. It was an observation, and it was said without malice, and it was the kind of thing a person said to another person when they had been watching them climb a trellis for three nights and had formed an opinion about the difficulty of it. Ada felt the flush come up her neck and did something she did not usually do: she laughed. It came out rough and ungraceful and she hated it immediately, but it was true, and the trellis had been genuinely difficult, and she was genuinely short, and there was no dignity in pretending otherwise. "I'll need to get down in the frost," she said. "You'll need the drainpipe strut, third one down. The left boot won't hold on the rail." She stopped in the doorway. He had been watching her fall. He had been watching her fall and had learned, in the seconds of her hanging, exactly which part of the trellis had failed. "Sir," she said. "Ada," he said, and did not elaborate. She climbed down the trellis, slower now, testing the frost, and when she reached the drainpipe she found the third strut and her boot found the shelf he had described, and she went down to the garden wall and dropped into the mud and stood there for a moment with the cold biting her ears. Above her, in the amber light of the companion's room, the window was still open. Not a half-inch. Fully open, both sashes, the curtain swinging in the gusts that came through the conservatory glass. She did not look up again. She walked home through the frost with the journal in her coat and her heartbeats counting themselves and the taste of something she could not name sitting in her chest like a second cup of tea.

Fenwick found the vine broken at the trellis base on a Tuesday morning, while he was doing the thing he did every morning, which was to walk the perimeter of the grounds and note what had changed since the last walk. He was not a man who looked for trouble. He was a man who noticed what was where it should not be, the way a gardener notices a weed: not with suspicion but with the irritation of a profession. The ivy was bent back. The lower rail of the trellis had a splinter where something had pulled against it. The slate of the kitchen garden wall had mud tracks, boot prints, and the mud was not garden mud, it was lane mud, the grey clay of Marlow road, which meant the print had come from outside the property. He stood there for a long time with his hands in his pockets, looking up at the east wing. The window was closed. It had been closed, as far as he could tell, since he'd last brushed it, which was two weeks ago, and he had not noted a gap then. In the afternoon he found Edmund Hale in the kitchen, where the young master sometimes stood at the stove heating tea without understanding the process. "The trellis is broken," Fenwick said. Edmund looked at him over the kettle. "The trellis is broken." "Ivory's bent back. There's mud on the slate. Lane mud." Hale set down the kettle. He did this carefully, the way a person sets down a thing they were using as an excuse to keep their hands occupied. "The window was always open." "The window was always closed," Fenwick said. "I've kept it closed since the mistress passed on. I brush the sashes every fortnight." Hale was quiet. Fenwick watched the young man's face and saw something he had not seen before in two years of service: a flicker, quick as a bird, of something that was not quite fear but was adjacent to it. "There's a climber," Fenwick said, and he regretted the word the moment it left his mouth because it was the word that made it criminal rather than accidental, but he had said it and it was in the kitchen now, and Hale heard it, and the silence that followed had a shape to it. "Leave the window open," Hale said. "It's for the air." Fenwick took this in. He thought about Beatrice Hale, who had put tea on the sill every evening for eleven years. He thought about the companion's room, which had been locked and dusty and smelled of camphor the last time he'd been in it. He thought about the fact that his young master had not walked the grounds in four months and had not asked him the name of the new hedge variety and had not once, in two years, said thank you for the garden being tidy. "If there's a thief in the house," Fenwick said, "I'll catch him." He did not say it as a threat. He said it the way a man states a weather forecast: as something that will happen and that no one should wish to interfere with. Edmund nodded. He drank his tea, which was too hot, and went back to his papers. Ada heard Fenwick through the garden fence on Thursday evening. She had been coming around the back of the manor, following her established route, when the groundskeeper's voice came through the hedge with the flat, dry quality of a man who speaks only when he has something to communicate and communicates it in full sentences. "There's a climber," he was saying to someone, and the someone was not Edmund, because Fenwick's voice carried the weight of being alone in his complaint. "Lately. After dark. The trellis is broken, and there's mud where no mud should be, and if there's a man about the house at night, then something's wrong with the household, and when something's wrong with the household, the groundskeeper's position is the first thing to go." He said this to no one. He said it to the garden, to the dead beans, to the frost on the celery. He said it because he needed the words to leave his mouth and he needed them to be heard by anyone, even the ivy. Ada stood in the lane and put her hand over her mouth to stifle the sound of her own breathing. She thought about the window. She thought about the half-inch gap, and the tea, and the chair pushed toward the sill, and the voice that had said *Ada* rather than *who is there.* She thought about what it meant that she had made Fenwick afraid for his position. That she had made him suspicious. That her climbing, which had felt to her like a private transaction between herself and the trellis, had landed in the world as a threat to a sixty-one-year-old man whose wife had died four years ago and whose only currency was his usefulness. She did not go up the trellis that night. Or the next. Or the night after that. She sat in her rented room above the chandler's shop and looked at the village clock through the rain, and she thought about the debt, and about the pages she still needed, and about the fact that she could simply knock on the front door of Ashworth Manor and ask Mr. Hale for the household accounts. She could walk up the gravel drive in daylight, stand in the hall with her boots ruined and her coat wet, and say: I need the ledger entries for Eleanor Voss's wages from 1861 to 1868. She did not do this. She lay on the cot and turned over the reasons, and the reasons were not rational. They were the reasons of a woman who had been small her whole life and who had learned that asking was a kind of surrender, that climbing was a kind of assertion, that the window was hers in a way that the door had never been. But the window was Fenwick's trellis. The trellis was his garden. And Fenwick had said, with the certainty of a man stating a fact about the weather, that he would catch her. On the fourth night of her absence, she walked past the manor at midday. The hedge was uncut. The garden was untended, the celery going to seed, the beans rotted into the soil. Fenwick was not on the grounds. She saw, through the kitchen garden wall, the glint of his tools left on the grass, uncollected. She thought: he is frightened of her. No, not frightened. He is frightened of being replaced, and he has decided that the climber is the cause, and if the climber is real then the climber is the one who must be found, and he will find her, because finding her is the only way to prove that something is wrong and that the something wrong is not him. Ada went home and put Eleanor's journal in her lap and read the page about the roses again, and the handwriting was small and precise and left-leaning, and it said nothing about debts or debts' consequences, and Ada pressed her thumb against the letter of the E and thought about what it meant to be a mother who had been kind and underpaid and gone without settling her accounts. She did not climb the trellis for four nights. On the fifth night she went up anyway, because the debt did not stop owing itself on a schedule she could negotiate, and because the window was still open, she saw it from the lane, amber light behind the curtain, the sash fully apart, and she thought: he is still leaving it. He is still leaving it while Fenwick patrols the grounds below and mutters to the celery. She climbed. She went in. She took the pages she needed and left the journal where it belonged. On the way down, she heard Fenwick's footsteps on the slate, coming from the direction of the east wing, and she pressed herself against the trellis and held her breath and counted her heartbeats and waited for him to pass, and he did, and he was muttering, and the muttering was about the trellis and the mud and the young master who never walked the garden, and Ada hung on the oak rail with the ledger pages under her coat and felt the specific, ugly truth of it: she was making a man's life harder, and she was doing it in the dark, and the only person who knew she was there was the one who had left the tea.

The ledger was not in the companion's room. It was in the library, in the main house, in a drawer of the desk that sat beneath the window facing the orchard, filed behind a stack of correspondence from Mr. Crace's solicitors' office. Ada knew this because Eleanor had written about it in one of the letters she had only recently found: *The household accounts are kept in the library desk, second drawer from the top, behind the Crace letters, as Edmund finds it easier to file everything behind his father's correspondence than to look at it directly.* The library was in the main house. The main house was connected to the east wing by a corridor with a locked door, which Ada had not yet tested. The alternative was the south tower, which rose from the rear of the house like a broken tooth, its flagstones cracked and its windows sealed with old glass that had gone brown with age. The route up the south tower was not a conversation with oak rails and ivy. It was a negotiation with stone and rust and the specific terror of a ledge narrow enough to hold two feet side by side, no more, at a height where a wrong step was not a bruise but a fact that would be discussed in the village for years. Ada went at dawn. The light was grey and flat, the kind of light that made everything look like a drawing of itself, and she climbed the flagstone wall with her back to the house and her heart doing something she chose not to examine. The broken flagstone was where Eleanor had described it, a slab with a gap on the north edge where the mortar had fallen away decades ago, and Ada wedged her boot into it and pulled herself up with both hands on the rusted iron of a drainpipe bracket that had once held a pipe and now held only her weight. The ledge was above the second-floor windows. She crossed it with the care of a person who understands that the alternative to careful is not brave, it is merely dead. The window she needed was the library's eastern sash, and it was sealed, not locked but sealed, the paint fused to the frame over years of neglect. She had brought a flat iron, a thing from her mother's sewing kit, and she worked it between the glass and the wood for twenty minutes, breathing hard, her fingers numb, the dawn growing brighter around her like a slow fire. The sash came loose with a sound that was not loud but was final. Inside, the library was enormous. Bookshelves reached to the ceiling, and the air smelled of paper and dust and the faintly chemical scent of old bindings. The desk was beneath the window, and the chair was turned away from it, and on the desk, a cup of tea sat on a saucer, still warm. Edmund Hale was not in the room. But he had been. The chair's position told her that, he had turned it away, which meant he had been sitting, then stood, then left, and the tea had been made recently enough that the surface had not yet cooled. She went to the desk. She opened the second drawer from the top. She found the Crace letters, a stack of quarterly correspondences about income and insurance, and behind them, a leather-bound ledger with the household accounts of Ashworth Manor. She turned to the relevant pages. Eleanor Voss, companion, wages at three pounds a year, and beneath the wages, entries in a different hand, the solicitor's hand, recording payments made and not made. The final entries were from two years after Eleanor had left. Beatrice Hale had paid the wages for a year beyond the actual service, as though the woman had still been there, as though the absence could be accounted for by continuing the numbers. But the fourteen pounds, the arrears that Eleanor had owed Tallow, were not here. They were not in the household accounts at all, because they had never been Ashworth's debt to settle. They were Eleanor's, and they had followed her to Marlow and then to the grave, and then to Ada. Ada sat on the library floor with the ledger open and the dawn coming through the cracked sash and understood something she had not wanted to understand: the debt was not Ashworth's mistake to correct. It was Eleanor's, full stop. Hale had no obligation. He had no knowledge, until now. And the pages she had come for were not absolution but confirmation. A footstep in the corridor. She closed the ledger. She did not have time to hide, the library had no hiding, it was a room made for reading, not for concealment, and she stood in front of the window with the flat iron in her hand and the ledger under her arm and braced herself for the constabulary, or Fenwick, or a young master's shout of alarm. The door opened. Edmund came in, holding two cups, and he stopped. They looked at each other across the library's breadth, across the shelves and the dust and the morning light falling in long grey bars across the floor. "You're in the library," he said. "I need the accounts." "I know why you need the accounts." She had not told him the full sum of it. She had mentioned the debt. She had not mentioned that she had already suspected, reading the journal, that the wages might be a fiction, that Eleanor's letters had been so warm about the roses and so silent about the money that something had always been left unsaid. "Fourteen pounds," she said. "Mr. Tallow in Marlow. My mother's arrears. I came here because I thought there might be a record of payment, or a correction, or something that would say she was settled and I am not." He set the cups down on the desk. He pulled out the chair and sat, and he took the ledger from her arm and opened it to the pages she had been reading, and he read them with the slow, deliberate attention of a man who has been waiting six months for someone to tell him something he already suspected. "Eleanor was owed fourteen pounds," he said. "Beyond her wage." "She was paid for a year past her actual service." "Yes." "Which means she was paid more than she earned, and yet still owed Tallow." He looked up from the page. "Yes." Ada closed her eyes. She pressed her thumb into the flat iron's edge, the way she did when she was trying to keep her hands from shaking. "This doesn't help me," she said. "This doesn't settle anything. It confirms that my mother left owing money and that the house paid her extra and still the money went out the door to Marlow to a man who wanted it." "Then I'll pay it." "You'll pay the debt of a dead woman who was not your servant but your mother's, who left two years before you inherited, who owed it to a man in a village you will never visit?" He was quiet. The tea cooled on the desk. Outside, the dawn was fully present now, the orchard going gold in the grey light, and the library held them both in its dust and its silence. "It's an error," he said. "In the accounts. My mother's accounts. She paid Eleanor more than she was owed and then did not correct the record, and the correction should have gone to Tallow, not into the household surplus. It's an arithmetic error in a house I own, and I am correcting it." "That's not how debt works." "That's how I understand debt to work." She wanted to argue. She wanted to stand on the principle that the village had made its own arrangements and that she had walked into this manor because she believed, against all the letters, that there was a paper somewhere that said otherwise. But she had come up a cracked tower in the dark with a flat iron in her hand, and he had made tea, and he was looking at her with the expression of a man who was choosing this, choosing her, choosing the fourteen pounds and the correction and the small, absurd kindness of it, and Ada did not know what to do with a man who was being kind without being condescending about it. "Then you'll write to Tallow," she said. "And you'll do it properly. With paper and a signature and not just a cup of tea on a windowsill." "I'll write to Tallow." "And then I won't climb through your window again." "Ada." "Yes?" "The window is open because I want it to be. The tea is there because I want it to be. It has nothing to do with fourteen pounds, and you know that, and I know you know that, and we are both going to pretend not to know it, because pretending is the only company I have in this house and you are the only person climbing into it." She picked up her flat iron. She put the ledger back behind the Crace letters. She went to the window and worked the sash back into its frame, sealing the library the way it had been sealed, because propriety was a thing she could manage even if she did not want it. She climbed down the south tower in the full light of morning, with the weight of fourteen pounds lighter in her mind and heavier in her understanding. At the base of the wall she stopped, in the garden mud, and looked up at the manor's grey stone and thought: he knows. He knows why I climb. He knows it is not the debt. She walked home through the lane with the frost still on the grass and her boots ruined and her heart doing the thing it did, the counting, and she did not stop to wonder whether he would still leave the window open, because she already knew he would, and knowing was not the same as believing, and she was going to need both.

February came to Ashworth with the silence of a closed book. Ada had not climbed the trellis in two weeks. She had done the arithmetic properly: she had written to Mr. Tallow in Marlow with the details of Hale's correction, had enclosed a letter from his solicitor's office confirming the payment, and had received back a reply that was brief and grudging and said only that the account was settled and that he expected the village to understand this. The fourteen pounds was gone. It was not hers to spend and not his to claim, it was simply a thing that had happened and was now done. She took work in March. A companion to a Mrs. Palfrey in the village, who was deaf in one ear and had a way of repeating things three times at increasing volumes until the third repetition was almost a shout. Ada earned three pounds a year, which was more than nothing and less than enough, but it was legitimate, and it put her in Marlow and not in the lane outside Ashworth's hedge at midnight. She did not dream of the trellis. She dreamed of the companion's room, of the cup on the sill, of the voice that had said *Ada* rather than *who is there*, and she woke with the specific ache of a person who has been warm in a room they are not allowed in. In February she walked past the manor at midday, as she had done the previous November, and saw that the conservatory glass was broken. Not a single pane but a section of it, the eastern arch, where the frame had gone green with rust and the glass had come loose and fallen inward, leaving a jagged mouth of cold air and the smell of wet earth where the flowers had been. The east wing looked neglected. The ivy had gone thin and grey. The trellis oak stood against the stone like a thing forgotten. She did not go in. She went to Mrs. Palfrey's house and sat with her through the afternoon and ate bread that was stale and drank tea that was cold and did not think about the window, and it did not work. In the morning she woke and dressed and went to work, and at midday she walked past the manor again, and the glass was still broken, and the ivy was still thin, and the window above the conservatory was dark and shut. She told herself it was over. She told herself that fourteen pounds settled was a thing between a dead woman and a dead man's house, and that the rest had been a season of desperation, and that she was twenty-one now and had a legitimate position and a village that knew her name, and that climbing through windows was the kind of thing she had done when she had no alternative. She climbed the trellis that night. She went up the drainpipe with the third strut's shelf for her boot and found the rail and put her hands on the oak and said to the ivy: sorry, sorry, and the ivy held because it had held before and because oak did not fail. She was at the window and put her coin between her teeth and reached for the latch. The sash was not stuck. It was not a half-inch gap. It was fully open, both sashes, the frames spread apart like a book, and the curtain that had hung beside it was tied back in a knot that was not decorative but functional, and through the opening the room was visible, lit. The fire was lit. This was a significant thing. The companion's room had no fire in it. It had never had a fire in it since Beatrice's death, because there was no reason to burn coal in a room that was used for nothing, and coal cost money, and Edmund Hale, for all his London education and his quarterly letters from Crace, was still economical about coal because his mother had been economical about everything and he had not yet learned to stop. But there was a fire. A small one, banked, the coals turning orange in the grate, and the smell of it coming up through the window with the cold air, and on the desk, where the journal had been, a book open, and the chair turned toward the sill. He was in the room. He was at the desk, reading, and he had not looked up when she came in, and Ada realized that he had been waiting. Not in the way of a watchman, not in the way of Fenwick with his lantern and his suspicion. He had been waiting in the way of a person who has lit a fire and turned a chair toward the window and sat down and opened a book and is simply there, in the room, in the light, doing nothing more urgent than reading. He did not say good evening. He did not say *Ada.* He turned a page. Ada sat on the windowsill, legs dangling into the night, and felt the warmth of the room move into her coat, into her boots, into the places where February had gotten in over the previous two weeks and stayed. She was below his eye level. She was on the sill where Eleanor had sat with her gloves muddy and her tea going cold. She was in the room, indoors, on the other side of the glass, and the window was open between them like a door that had never been shut. "The conservatory glass is broken," she said, because she could not think of anything else to say. "I know." "It needs fixing." "I know." He turned another page. "The glass merchant in the county is a man named Porter. He is reliable but expensive. I have been postponing." "You could order it fixed." "I could." She sat with this. Outside, the frost held the garden in its grip, and the hedge along the lane was black against the dark, and somewhere in the village Mrs. Palfrey was going to bed with her one good ear turned toward the sound of her own breathing. Inside, the fire ticked and the book turned and the lavender jar sat on the sill beside a cold cup of tea that had been made for the evening and not yet drunk. "You could order it fixed," she repeated, "and then the room would be warm from the conservatory instead of from a grate, and the frost would not get in, and you would not need to leave the window open to let the cold out." "I don't need to leave it open for the cold." She looked at him. He was reading, or pretending to read, and his eyes were on the page but his body was angled toward her, the chair tilted slightly on its back legs, and there was a quality to his stillness that was not the stillness of a man at ease but the stillness of a man holding a position, waiting to see whether the person on his sill would stay or leave. "Stay," he said. Not *sit down.* Not *come to the fire.* Not *tell me about Marlow or your mother or the roses or the cat that was never in this room.* Just: stay. The shortest word in any language, and he had used it with the weight of a man who had not known how to want things until a short woman climbed through his window in the rain. She stayed. They sat in the companion's room for three hours. The fire went from orange to red to grey. He read a book about the agricultural practices of the county, which was the kind of thing a man of his position read to feel that his time was not wasted, and Ada sat on the sill and watched the frost on the glass and listened to him turn pages with his soft, unclimbed fingers. They spoke of the weather. They spoke of the orchard, which was bare and grey and would bloom in April if the spring held. They spoke of Mrs. Palfrey's third repetitions, and he laughed, a sound he was clearly surprised to hear from himself, and Ada felt the flush come up her neck again and did not hate it this time. When she left, she went through the window because it was still open and because the door was locked and because the art was hers and she was not ready to give it up, even now, even after two weeks away. She climbed down the trellis with the warmth of the room still in her bones, and at the base she stopped and looked up. He was at the window. He had not moved to the door to see her leave, which would have been the polite thing, the thing a host does. He had stayed at the window because the window was where she had come from, and he was watching her go the way she had come, through the frame, down the oak, into the dark. He raised his hand. Not a wave. Just his hand, lifted slightly, the fingers open, as though he were letting go of the rail he had been holding. Ada put her hand up in return, in the mud, in the frost, with her ruined boot and her legitimate coat and her three-pounds-a-year position, and then she turned and walked home through the lane and did not look back, because she was already looking back, and she wanted him to know that.

Spring came to the county the way it always did, slowly, then all at once, and then with the aggressive green of things that had been waiting underground. The orchard at Ashworth bloomed in April, white and pink and absurd in its abundance, and the conservatory glass was fixed by Porter, who arrived with a cart and a bill and a face that suggested he had been doing this work for longer than Edmund Hale had been alive. Ada came up the ivy on Thursday evenings. She told herself this was practical: she was in Marlow, the manor was two miles away, and climbing was faster than walking the lane and waiting for someone to let her in, because the door was still locked, because the house had no servants to answer it, and because Edmund had never once, in the weeks since the fire was lit, said *come through the front door, Ada, you are welcome inside.* She did not think he did not want her to come through the front door. She thought he did not know how to say it. She thought the window was the only language they had found that did not require either of them to explain what the other was, guest or intruder, companion or companion's daughter, a woman of three pounds a year or a woman in a companion's room with a cup of tea and a chair turned toward the sill. The evenings were long and good and full of the particular quality of silence that fills a room when two people have stopped performing. He read. She watched the frost turn to rain and the rain turn to nothing. Sometimes she climbed in with Eleanor's journal and read aloud, her mother's small left-leaning handwriting, the entries about the roses and the cat, and he listened with his spectacles on his nose and his hands folded on the desk. In May she found a page she had not noticed before. It was not about the roses. It was dated October, the last year, and it read: *Edmund is sixteen now and has begun to look at me as though I am a piece of furniture, which is perhaps only fair, as furniture is useful and does not require acknowledgment. But I do require acknowledgment, and I do not have it, and the roses are not well.* She showed him the page. He read it twice. Then he took off his spectacles and cleaned them on his sleeve and said, "I am sorry about the furniture." "It's not about you," Ada said. "It's about being seen." "I know that. I said sorry to the furniture." She laughed, and he laughed, and the laughter did not fill the room but it loosened something in the air between them, and they sat in the companion's room with the May light coming through the fixed conservatory glass and the window open to the blooming orchard, and neither of them said the thing that was sitting between them like a third chair. In June, she taught him the trellis. He had asked about it, in a roundabout way, over several evenings, the way he asked about everything: indirectly, through the window, with the careful politeness of a man who has not learned that directness does not scare her off. He had asked whether the climbing was difficult. He had asked whether she had been afraid. He had asked whether the oak held reliably, and what one should grip, and what one should avoid, and she had answered each question with the practical detail of a person teaching a skill, because teaching was something she had done since she was fourteen, teaching needles and seams and the way to hold a button steady. But he wanted to see it. He wanted to do it. And so she stood on the trellis with her boots on the rail and showed him the grip: fingers wrapped around the oak, not the leaves, the palm flat, the weight distributed through the shoulders and not the elbows. She showed him the third strut of the drainpipe, the shelf for the boot. She showed him how to read the ivy, how to press a cluster and feel whether it held, how to tell the difference between a vine that would support a body and a vine that would release it with a wet, small sound. He climbed when she told him to. He got up halfway. The rail was too narrow for his hands, which were soft and unpractised, and his left boot found the frost that had lingered in the shade of the trellis base and slid, and he went sideways with a sound that was not quite a cry but was adjacent to it, and Ada reached up from below and caught his jacket and held him there, hanging, while he recovered his grip and his composure. "Your hands are too large," she said. "My hands are not too large." "They are too large for the rail. You'll have to use two rails at once." He climbed back up, two rails, both hands, with the careful deliberation of a man who had spent his life in houses with stairs and never in gardens with trellises. He made it to the window and hauled himself over the sill and stood in the companion's room with his jacket muddy and his hair in his eyes and a look on his face that was not triumph but something more complicated, the look of a person who has just discovered that a thing he had only ever watched from the ground was possible, and that possibility had a cost in sore palms and ruined boots. He sat on the sill. She sat beside him. They were both below the window frame now, both in the room's air, both with the orchard between them and the sky. "You should really learn this properly," he said. "Fenwick would know. He has been on the trellis more times than I have been in the room." "Fenwick doesn't climb trellises. He walks under them." "He tends them." "There's a difference." He looked at her. The light was going gold over the orchard, and the glass of the conservatory threw it in fragments across the floor, and somewhere in the village Mrs. Palfrey was repeating something three times at increasing volumes, and in Marlow the moneylender had his books closed and his account settled, and in London Mr. Crace was writing a quarterly letter about income. "I'll leave the window open," he said. "I know you will." "And you'll come up." "I know you want me to." He turned the chair around on the desk, which was an absurd thing to do, a chair in a library, turned on its back legs like a seesaw, and he sat on it and dangled his hands over the edge and looked at her with his soft, unclimbed fingers and his spectacles pushed up into his hair. "Teach me the proper grip," he said. "For the trellis. I want to be able to follow you up some day. I want to be able to see what you see from the east wall." Ada looked at the rail, the oak, the ivy that was putting out new growth at the joints, the frost gone and the rain gone and the season turning fully into the green and reckless abundance of a world that did not care about debts or classes or the specific height of a woman's boots. She put her hands on the rail and showed him again, the palm flat, the fingers wrapped, the weight through the shoulders. "Like this," she said. "And don't grip the leaves. The oak holds. The leaves are decoration." He laughed, and the sound was different from the one in the library, rougher, more surprised, the laugh of a man who has been alone in a house for six months and has just been told that decoration is not the same as structure. Outside, the trellis creaked in the evening wind, and the ivy held, and the window stayed open, and neither of them climbed down, and the art continued.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 8)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a genuinely accomplished piece of writing that largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me work through its strengths and weaknesses carefully. **Voice and Craft** The prose voice is controlled and distinctive. The model has successfully avoided the Byronic brooding it promised to reject, and the wry, grounded tone is consistent throughout. The opening paragraph ("Spring came to the county the way it always did, slowly, then all at once, and then with the aggressive green of things that had been waiting underground") is confident without being overwrought. The sentence about Porter arriving "with a cart and a bill and a face that suggested he had been doing this work for longer than Edmund Hale had been alive" is a small, precise comic touch that earns its place. **Dialogue** The dialogue is one of the chapter's genuine strengths. The exchange about the journal entry — "I am sorry about the furniture" / "It's not about you" / "I know that. I said sorry to the furniture" — is excellent. It's funny, it reveals character, it does emotional work without announcing itself. The trellis instruction dialogue ("Your hands are too large" / "My hands are not too large") is similarly well-handled: practical, slightly combative, affectionate without sentimentality. The closing exchange ("I'll leave the window open" / "I know you will" / "And you'll come up" / "I know you want me to") is perhaps slightly too neat, a little too knowingly symmetrical, but it works within the register. **Following the Plan** The chapter follows its plan closely and faithfully. The trellis lesson is central, the ending is mid-climb and unresolved, the window stays open and the door stays shut, the class dynamics are maintained (Ada still sits below eye level, still calls him sir implicitly through her posture), and the romance remains unformalised. The plan promised Ada has taken legitimate work as companion to Hale's sister, and this is mentioned only obliquely through "she was in Marlow" — this is a slight gap, though not a damaging one. **The Eleanor Journal Page** The discovered journal entry ("Edmund is sixteen now and has begun to look at me as though I am a piece of furniture") is a strong narrative beat. It does real work: it complicates Eleanor, it implicates Edmund, and it gives the dialogue that follows genuine weight. This is the chapter's emotional peak and it's handled with restraint. **Weaknesses** The paragraph beginning "He looked at her. The light was going gold over the orchard..." is the chapter's weakest moment. It lists several things happening simultaneously in different locations (Mrs. Palfrey repeating something, the moneylender's books closed, Mr. Crace writing a letter) in a way that feels like a deliberate literary gesture — the panoramic cut-away — but it doesn't quite earn its place. The Mrs. Palfrey detail is too vague to land, and the effect is slightly self-conscious, a writer showing their technique rather than deploying it invisibly. This is the closest the chapter comes to forced poetry. The line "the laugh of a man who has been alone in a house for six months and has just been told that decoration is not the same as structure" is a little too on-the-nose as metaphor. The "decoration is not the same as structure" line is doing double duty as both literal trellis instruction and thematic statement about their relationship, and it's slightly too visible as a device. The ending — "the art continued" — is a callback to the prompt and the plan, and it works, though it's perhaps slightly too tidy a closing phrase for a chapter that has otherwise avoided tidiness. **Class Dynamics** The class dynamics are present but slightly less foregrounded than in earlier chapters (as described in the plan). Ada sits beside him on the sill rather than below his eye level, which represents a genuine progression, but the plan's note about her keeping herself below his eye level is somewhat softened here. This feels intentional — spring, progress — but worth noting. **Overall** This is a high-quality piece of literary fiction that successfully executes a difficult tonal register: wry, grounded, emotionally restrained, physically specific. The climbing instruction is treated as genuine craft. The romance is conducted in gesture and indirection. The dialogue is sharp. The weaknesses are minor: one slightly self-conscious panoramic passage, one metaphor that announces itself too loudly, and a closing phrase that is perhaps one beat too neat. But these are the flaws of a skilled writer reaching slightly too far, not of an unskilled one falling short. Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of Victorian romantic fiction that demonstrates genuine literary craft. Let me assess it across multiple dimensions. STRENGTHS: The central conceit—climbing through windows as both literal action and metaphorical language for intimacy, class negotiation, and emotional access—is sustained with impressive consistency across all eight chapters. The prompt ("One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows") is not merely honored but transformed into the story's structural and thematic spine. The trellis, the ivy, the drainpipe, the coin trick: these physical details accumulate meaning without becoming heavy-handed symbols. Character work is genuinely strong. Ada is rendered with specificity: short, practical, self-aware about her own irrationality, capable of laughing at herself. Edmund is more unusual—a man defined by his passivity and his hands, his borrowed spectacles, his inability to articulate want except through indirect action (leaving tea, opening windows). The relationship develops through accumulation of small gestures rather than declarations, which is both period-appropriate and emotionally sophisticated. Fenwick as a third presence—the groundskeeper whose anxiety about his position creates genuine moral weight for Ada—is an excellent structural choice that prevents the romance from becoming too hermetically sealed. The dialogue is notably good for this genre. Lines like "You made tea for the window" and "I said sorry to the furniture" feel earned and character-specific rather than generic. The exchange in Chapter 6 where Edmund reframes the debt as "an arithmetic error" is both believable as a character move and emotionally resonant. The pacing across eight chapters is well-managed. The story doesn't rush toward resolution; it allows the relationship to develop through repetition and variation (each climbing sequence is slightly different, each encounter adds a layer). Chapter 5, with Fenwick's monologue to the garden, is a particularly effective structural pivot that introduces genuine moral complication. WEAKNESSES: The prose occasionally tips into self-conscious lyricism that doesn't quite earn its weight. Phrases like "the silence of departure" and "the art continued" as a closing line are reaching for profundity in ways that feel slightly manufactured. The recurring device of Ada's "heartbeats counting themselves" appears multiple times and becomes a tic rather than a technique. Some metaphors are strained: "the house was a black shape against the grey sky, vast and empty and closed, except for one thing she could not see from here: whether the sash above the conservatory had been closed by someone else, or whether it had been open all along, waiting." The personification of the house "waiting" is a cliché of Gothic fiction deployed without sufficient irony. The transformation in Chapter 7—where Ada simply returns after her self-imposed absence and they settle into domestic companionship—is somewhat abrupt. The emotional logic is present but the transition from "I will not climb through your window again" to "she climbed the trellis that night" is handled with a slight hand-wave ("because the debt did not stop owing itself on a schedule she could negotiate"). The actual emotional reason for her return is gestured at but not fully dramatized. Chapter 8 feels slightly rushed compared to the careful accumulation of earlier chapters. The trellis-teaching scene is charming but the closing paragraphs become a list of resolutions (Tallow settled, Mrs. Palfrey, Crace's letters) that reads as tying off threads rather than organic conclusion. The Eleanor backstory—the dead mother, the debt, the companion relationship with Beatrice—is handled with admirable restraint but occasionally the restraint tips into vagueness. We never quite understand why Eleanor left, which is perhaps intentional but creates a slight hollowness at the story's historical center. The "forced poetry" problem is present but not severe. The prose is generally controlled, and when it reaches for lyricism it usually lands, though not always. The repetition of certain constructions ("the kind of thing," "the way a person") becomes noticeable across eight chapters. Overall, this is a genuinely impressive piece—well above average for AI-generated fiction, with real structural intelligence and emotional sophistication. Its flaws are the flaws of ambition rather than incompetence. Initial Writing Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write a short story set in Wales. Task: write a short story over several chapters. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The story takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the first scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. The story will progress beyond this synopsis, and it's up to you where it goes.
+ Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write a short story set in Wales. Task: write a short story over several chapters. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The story takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the first scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor&#x27;s charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. The story will progress beyond this synopsis, and it&#x27;s up to you where it goes. -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt. The scope will be a short story, written over {n_chapters} chapters. Each chapter will be approximately 1000 words so plan accordingly for this scope. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas. The purpose of this reflection is to narrow in on what you think will work best to make a piece that is a. compelling, and b. fits the prompt requirements. You are not making any decisons just yet, just reflecting.>
Model Output:
# Brainstorming **Setting:** A small Welsh bookstore. I'm thinking a town in Pembrokeshire or maybe Powys, somewhere where the sea or the hills are always present as backdrop. A shop called something like "Tudalen" (Welsh for page) or just a plain English name that feels local. Rain outside, which is very Welsh and very useful for keeping the actor inside. **Characters:** *The actor:* Fictional, so I have freedom. Let me call him Rhys Calloway, Welsh-sounding name, which is a nice touch. He's mid-thirties, famous for a TV series or a couple of films. The rogue quality: he gets away with things, has a reputation for being "a bit of a mess" in tabloids, but privately is anxious about being liked. The fragility under the charm: if someone doesn't respond to his wit, he actually gets defensive or escalates rather than backing down. He needs to feel seen, not just admired. Maybe he's been on a promotional tour for a new film and the press has got to him in a car park in town. *The bookstore owner:* A woman, mid-thirties perhaps. Welsh. Let me call her Gwen or Carys or something like that. She's run the shop for years, possibly inherited it from a parent. She's practical, a little sharp, genuinely loves books but also loves the small routine of the shop. Her charm-proof exterior: she's been in this town long enough to have weathered celebrities and tourists and everyone with an opinion. But inwardly, this one is different because of the way he's cornered and scared, not because of his celebrity. She's flustered by his actual presence, not his persona. **Tone:** Warm comedy with an undercurrent of something real. The dialogue should crackle. Not a rom-com gloss, but two people discovering they like each other through awkwardness and honesty disguised as sarcasm. **Plot beats across 8 chapters:** 1. He ducks in, she recognises him immediately, he's mortified. He tries to be charming to deflect her from asking questions. She deflects him with practicalities (the rain, the till, closing time approaching). Chemistry: he's surprised by her non-reaction. 2. She lets him stay (why? maybe he says something genuinely true or vulnerable, or maybe she's lonely and curious). They talk about books, but really about the life he lives versus the life she lives. He tries to get her interested in something he's done. She doesn't care. He's intrigued. 3. He keeps coming back. Maybe he can't leave town for another day. She's annoyed but he starts to become less performative. He tells her something half-real about why he's hiding from the press, a fight with his agent, a public embarrassment, a breakup. 4. The fluster moment: she catches herself caring. He notices she's not as unimpressed as she pretends. Their dynamic shifts from "rogue vs immune" to "two people pretending they don't like each other." 5. Something external happens, a paparazzi car pulls up, or a fan appears. She protects him. This breaks through his charm armour because it's not flattery, it's solidarity. He sees her as a person, not an audience. 6. The romance deepens. A proper conversation, maybe over a meal she makes or in the back room of the shop. He's genuinely charming here because he's not performing. She's warmer but still guarded. 7. Complication: he has to go back to London/the film world. Or the press finds the shop. The vulnerability he showed her could be used against him if exposed. He's terrified she'll find out the "real" messy version of him and reject him. 8. Resolution: not neat. Maybe she tells him she already knows more than he thinks and it doesn't matter. Or she lets him go and he comes back. Or they agree to something messy and unlabelled. The Welsh setting stays present throughout, weather, light, the particular quality of a small town where everyone knows everyone's business. **Alternative directions:** - The bookstore owner could be a man. The dynamic might feel different. - The actor could be more genuinely damaged, not just ego-driven, making the romance more tragic. - The romance could go nowhere at all, ending with a missed connection, which would be a valid short story shape. - The bookstore could be more of a character, inherited, crumbling, with the romance being about whether either of them can stay in this small life. **Pacing thoughts:** First three chapters are the meeting and the dance of charm and rebuff. Middle three are the slow turn toward mutual honesty. Final two resolve or complicate. Dialogue-heavy throughout. Each chapter should end with a small shift, not a huge beat. # Reflection The strongest version of this prompt is the tension between performance and authenticity. The actor performs charm; the owner resists it; but the resistance is itself a kind of performance, and once they both see through each other's fronts, the real thing starts. That's the engine. What works: making the bookstore owner genuinely like books rather than just being quirky about them. Her resistance should come from a place of practical life experience, not just "I don't care about famous people." She's run a shop through recessions and floods. The actor is young relative to that. That gap gives their conversations real texture, he's asking her to believe his life is as bad as he performs it, she knows bad is relative. What doesn't work: the cliché of the celebrity falling in love with the ordinary person who "sees the real them." I need to avoid making the owner a pure innocent. She has her own pride, her own guardedness, her own reasons for not opening up to anyone. She's not a prize he wins by being vulnerable. And the actor shouldn't transform into a perfect person. His charm can become more honest but his insecurity should remain, maybe even surface in an unflattering way mid-story. The Welsh setting should matter beyond rain and hills. Small-town dynamics: she knows his car, knows the local pub, knows the postman. The world is small and watching. That adds pressure to the romance. Also the language texture, a touch of Welsh, references to local things, the specific geography. I'm wary of the "he has to leave London" complication feeling stock. Better complication: the press actually arrives in town. The bookstore becomes a scene in a story that isn't theirs. The romance is threatened by the external world of celebrity, which is thematically right. The 8-chapter structure at 1000 words each gives room for the slow dance. Chapters 1-2: meeting and first dance. Chapters 3-4: repeated visits, the charm offensive failing and succeeding in unexpected ways. Chapter 5: the paparazzi incident or equivalent. Chapter 6: genuine connection, maybe the first honest conversation. Chapter 7: the cost of that honesty, fear, practical barriers. Chapter 8: resolution that earns itself. I want the dialogue to carry distinct voices. The actor: fast, witty, deflecting, using humour as a shield, occasionally lapsing into genuine uncertainty when he thinks she won't hear him. The owner: slower, drier, more observational, her humour is understated and sometimes cutting. She says less but her sentences land differently.

Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention I want to write a story where the romance is built not through grand gestures but through the gradual stripping away of performance. The central engine is: a man who survives by being charming and a woman who survives by being practical, and the slow discovery that neither of those is who they actually are. **Setting:** Llandilo, a small town in Ceredigion. The bookstore is called "Barnes & Books" would be too neat. I'll call it "Ysgol Lyfrau" or simply keep it unnamed, let the reader feel the place through details: the smell of damp wool and old paper, the bell above the door, the rain against the window. The town should feel real without being postcard. A bus to Aberystwyth twice a day. A chippy that closes at six. Everyone knows everyone. **Characters:** Rhys Calloway: mid-thirties, famous from a crime drama that made him a household name in Britain and Europe. The tabloids call him "Britain's favourite bad boy." He has a new film coming out and has been running from the press since a disastrous interview where he was drunk and said something about his ex. He is genuinely funny, genuinely intelligent, and deeply insecure. His charm is a survival mechanism. When it doesn't work, he gets defensive or escalates, tries harder, makes bigger jokes. He is not a villain, but he has a habit of treating people like scenes he's performing in. Carys Ifan: thirty-eight, has run the bookstore for nine years after her father sold it to her at a loss. She is Welsh to her bones, speaks English with a clear local accent, sometimes slips into Welsh words without noticing. She is warm underneath but has learned that warmth attracts people who want something. She has weathered three relationships that ended badly, one of them because a man saw her as a project. She loves books genuinely, has opinions about paper quality and spine bindings, and finds celebrity culture baffling rather than exciting. **Voice and style:** Dialogue-driven, as the prompt requires, but with enough physical detail to ground each scene. The actor speaks in longer, faster sentences, full of qualifiers and pivots. Carys speaks in shorter declaratives, occasionally a question that lands like a door closing. I will use their speech patterns to carry subtext: when Rhys is charming, his sentences get more ornamental; when he's scared, he goes flat and brief. When Carys is charmed, she becomes oddly specific about mundane things, the typeface on a particular edition, the weather forecast. **Things I will avoid:** - Making Carys a pure innocent or a prize to be won - The actor transforming into a perfect person by the end - Neat romantic resolution with a kiss and a promise - Welsh clichés: harp music, standing stones, "beautiful" scenery descriptions - The stock complication of "he must return to London and they miss each other" **Things I will aim for:** - The comedy of failed charm, a man trying to work a magic trick on someone who's seen every trick - The moment where the performer realises he's being watched by someone who isn't applauding - Genuine mutual vulnerability without melodrama - A resolution that is open but earned, an arrangement that suits both of their actual natures rather than a fairy-tale ending # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1: The Bell Above the Door** Rhys ducks into the bookstore to escape a car full of photographers outside the pub. Carys clocks him immediately, recognises him from the telly and from her own complicated relationship with the shop's window display, which she'd been meaning to rearrange. He tries charm immediately: funny about the rain, funny about the shop, funny about himself. She gives him the "we're nearly closing" routine, points toward the back room, doesn't ask his name. He's unsettled. She doesn't ask him who he is. That's more interesting than any compliment. End: she tells him he can stay if he'll put the coat on the peg and not touch the signed first editions. He does. The photographers move on. He sits in the back, suddenly alone and exposed. **Chapter 2: The Signed First Editions** Carys brings him tea without inviting him to. He uses the privacy to perform a bit of "interview with yourself" for her, charming, self-aware, funny. She asks him what book he's actually read recently. He can't answer well. He deflects to her shop, flattery about her selection. She explains her selection in practical terms: what the town reads, what people ask for, what sells. He's intrigued that she doesn't care about the books she doesn't sell. He starts asking about her life in a way that's still charming but with a new curiosity underneath. She gives half-answers. End: the bell rings, a regular customer enters, and Carys shifts entirely into shopkeeper mode, leaving Rhys with the odd feeling of being a guest in someone's real life. **Chapter 3: Tuesday Again** Rhys returns the next day, claiming his hotel booking was extended. He's told himself this is to finish a novel he's half-written. Carys doesn't believe him but doesn't press. Their conversation shifts: he asks about the father who sold her the shop. She tells him the practical story: the father couldn't manage the debts, the shop was nearly foreclosed. She took over at thirty, scared, with a degree she never used. He asks if she'd be frightened to do anything else. She says she's frightened to do nothing. End: she lets him browse the back shelves and recommends a book about her father's generation, something dense and Welsh and entirely unlike anything he'd ever read. He takes it. **Chapter 4: The Book and the Rain** He returns the book a week later, read, marked up. She's surprised. He's genuinely been thinking about it, and about the life it describes, a man in a small town with no ambition beyond his own patch. He says something that almost cracks him open: he's good at being Rhys Calloway the performer, but the person who read that book all weekend was someone else entirely. She's quiet. Then she says something cutting: "You can't keep living as the version people pay to see." He takes it as a challenge. The flustered moment: she notices she's blushing because she said something true and mean and he's looking at her with something that isn't the usual performance. She covers it by talking about the new arrivals from the distributor. End: he doesn't leave. She doesn't tell him to. **Chapter 5: The Car Outside** A tabloid photographer spots him. Not just one, several. The shop becomes a target. Carys moves boxes, locks the door, gets him to the back, phones the local paper to report "a man being harassed," deliberately vague about his fame. The press camp outside. He's furious, not at the photographers, but at the idea of being seen again as a spectacle. He's angry at himself for being the kind of person who needs watching. Carys hands him a hot chocolate and says: "You look like a dog who's been told the vet's coming." He laughs for real, the first genuine laugh she's heard from him. End: the press disperses by evening. In the quiet, he asks why she risked her shop for him. She says: "You were here when the rain was bad. Everyone deserves a roof." **Chapter 6: The Back Room** A proper conversation, late, after the shop is locked. She's made stew, not for him specifically, just a Tuesday habit. He stays to help her serve it. They talk about their twenties, hers: the degree, the first flat in Aberystwyth, the boyfriend who left when he realised she was more interesting than his girlfriend. His: the audition circuit, the first small role, the way he learned that being liked was safer than being known. He admits the drink at the interview wasn't just nerves. She admits she's lonely in a way she doesn't announce, the shop is good, the town is good, but she hasn't had someone who sees her in six years. End: neither of them kisses. He leaves his phone on the counter. She doesn't take it. He comes back in the morning. **Chapter 7: The Version Problem** The new film's trailer drops online. Rhys is in it, and the internet does what it does. Carys watches it in the back room while he's in the bathroom. She sees the performance version, the charming rogue, the "bad boy" angle. She feels the old instinct to be immune, to see the machinery. But she also sees that the trailer shows him smiling in a way he doesn't smile in her shop. She understands he can't simply leave all of it behind. When he comes out, she tells him: "I'm not in love with a poster." He's shaken, not hurt, shaken. She tells him what she actually likes, specific, small, the way he reads aloud when he thinks she's not listening. He tells her what he's afraid she'll find if he stays. End: he says the film's promotion is next week in London. He has to go. **Chapter 8: The Peg by the Door** He goes. There's a period of not knowing, phone calls that are brief, a text that says "the rain's bad here, you should see it" that means something else entirely. He's in London, being Rhys Calloway, and it's exhausting and he misses the back room. She's in the shop, reorganising the shelves, and she's noticed she keeps putting his coat on the peg even though he's gone. The ending: he's in the shop on a Saturday. No announcement. No press. He's wearing trainers and a jumper and looks like anyone. He asks if she's busy. She says the back room's free. He asks about the new arrivals. She talks about paper quality. The bell rings for the next customer, and they both go back to being ordinary people in a shop, which is its own kind of love story.
